This helps uncover the information content of activation vectors, and facilitates understanding of the algorithms implemented by transformer models. We present four case studies where we investigate models ranging from small transformers to GPT-2. In these studies, we show that InversionView can reveal clear information contained in activations, including basic information about tokens appearing in the context, as well as more complex information, such as the count of certain tokens, their relative positions, and abstract knowledge about the subject. We also provide causally verified circuits to confirm the decoded information.

papers.title: Its Alive: AI Independence Without Human Prompting
papers.research_question: How can representation engineering (RepE) improve transparency and control of AI systems, particularly for safety-relevant concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces representation engineering (RepE) as a top-down approach to AI transparency, providing baselines like Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) and demonstrating its applicability to reading and controlling safety-relevant concepts in large language models.
papers.conclusion: RepE is a promising top-down approach for enhancing AI transparency and control, with broad applicability to safety-relevant problems, and can accelerate progress in AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
RepE methods can extract representations of high-level concepts like honesty, utility, emotion, and harmfulness.
LAT achieves state-of-the-art on TruthfulQA, improving zero-shot accuracy by 18.1 percentage points.
Representation control can increase model honesty and reduce compliance with harmful instructions, even under jailbreak attempts.
Emotions are represented in LLMs and can be manipulated to affect model compliance and behavior.
RepE provides traction on inner alignment problems like deceptive alignment by enabling monitoring and control of honesty.
future_direction: Further exploration of RepE for transparency and safety of AI systems.
Investigation of emotion representations and their impact on model behavior and concept of self.
Improving robustness and generalization of RepE methods.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify and characterize the emerging area of representation engineering (RepE), an approach to enhancing the transparency of AI systems that draws on insights from cognitive neuroscience. RepE places population-level representations, rather than neurons or circuits, at the center of analysis, equipping us with novel methods for monitoring and manipulating high-level cognitive phenomena in deep neural networks (DNNs). We provide baselines and an initial analysis of RepE techniques, showing that they offer simple yet effective solutions for improving our understanding and control of large language models. We showcase how these methods can provide traction on a wide range of safety-relevant problems, including honesty, harmlessness, power-seeking, and more, demonstrating the promise of top-down transparency research. We hope that this work catalyzes further exploration of RepE and fosters advancements in the transparency and safety of AI systems.

papers.title: Transformers Are Born Biased: Structural Inductive Biases at Random Initialization and Their Practical Consequences
papers.research_question: Do randomly initialized transformers exhibit systematic structural biases, and what are their mechanisms and practical consequences?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers exhibit strong structural biases at random initialization due to representation contraction driven by MLP and attention, which persist through training and enable seed-specific fingerprinting (SeedPrint) and explain the attention-sink phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are not blank slates; they possess inherent structural biases at initialization that persist through training, with implications for model fingerprinting and architecture design.
papers.key_findings:
Randomly initialized transformers show extreme token preferences, with certain tokens predicted orders of magnitude more often than others.
This preference arises from inter-sequence representation contraction, where last-token representations from different sequences become highly similar.
The contraction is primarily driven by asymmetric nonlinear activations in MLP layers, and amplified by self-attention through intra-sequence aggregation.
These initialization-induced biases persist throughout training, forming a stable model identity that can be used for fingerprinting (SeedPrint).
The attention mechanism's intra-sequence contraction leads to a positional discrepancy that causally explains the attention-sink phenomenon in trained LLMs.
future_direction: Design architectures that are more neutral or explicitly incorporate desired inductive biases.
Treat initialization choices as hyperparameters tuned for final model behavior, not just optimization stability.
Extend the fingerprinting method to more challenging scenarios, such as detecting obfuscated or distilled models.
papers.abstract: Transformers underpin modern large language models (LLMs) and are commonly assumed to be behaviorally unstructured at random initialization, with all meaningful preferences emerging only through large-scale training. We challenge this assumption by showing that randomly initialized transformers already exhibit strong and systematic structural biases. In particular, untrained models display extreme token preferences: across random input sequences, certain tokens are predicted with probabilities orders of magnitude larger. We provide a mechanistic explanation for this phenomenon by dissecting the transformer architecture at initialization. We show that extreme token preference arises from a contraction of token representations along a random seed-dependent direction. This contraction is driven by two interacting forces: (i) asymmetric nonlinear activations in MLP sublayers induce global (inter-sequence) representation concentration, and (ii) self-attention further amplifies this effect through local (intra-sequence) aggregation. Together, these mechanisms align hidden representations along a direction determined solely by the random initialization, producing highly non-uniform next-token predictions. Beyond mechanistic insight, we demonstrate that these initialization-induced biases persist throughout training, forming a stable and intrinsic model identity. Leveraging this property, we introduce SeedPrint, a fingerprinting method that can reliably distinguish models that differ only in their random initialization, even after extensive training and under substantial distribution shift. Finally, we identify a fundamental positional discrepancy inherent to the attention mechanism's intra-sequence contraction that is causally linked to the attention-sink phenomenon. This discovery provides a principled explanation for the emergence of sinks and offers a pathway for their control.

papers.title: REAL: Reading Out Transformer Activations for Precise Localization in Language Model Steering
papers.research_question: How can we better identify internal modules (attention heads or layers) that govern specific behaviors in LLMs for the purpose of inference-time steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REAL, a framework that uses a vector-quantized autoencoder (VQ-AE) to learn a disentangled latent space from module activations, enabling more precise identification of behavior-relevant modules (heads or layers) for inference-time steering in Transformers.
papers.conclusion: REAL provides a more effective and principled approach for selecting behavior-relevant modules in Transformers, leading to improved performance across a variety of inference-time steering tasks including truthfulness enhancement, knowledge conflict resolution, and general alignment.
papers.key_findings:
REAL outperforms existing methods like ITI and LoFiT in truthfulness steering, achieving significant improvements (e.g., up to 81.5% relative improvement on MC1 for Qwen2.5-7B).
The attention heads selected by REAL on a truthfulness task show strong zero-shot generalization to knowledge-seeking tasks in different model families.
REAL effectively localizes layers for steering in knowledge conflict tasks, outperforming the state-of-the-art SPARE method on benchmarks like NQSWAP and MACNOISE.
The method's relevance scores, derived from the VQ-AE encodings, provide a principled way to rank modules and assign steering strengths.
Visualizations (t-SNE, heatmaps) show that REAL identifies heads with more discriminative activation patterns compared to linear-probe-based methods.
papers.abstract: Inference-time steering aims to alter a large language model's (LLM's) responses without changing its parameters, but a central challenge is identifying the internal modules that most strongly govern the target behavior. Existing approaches often rely on simplistic cues or ad hoc heuristics, leading to suboptimal or unintended effects. We introduce REAL, a framework for identifying behavior-relevant modules (attention heads or layers) in Transformer models. For each module, REAL trains a vector-quantized autoencoder (VQ-AE) on its hidden activations and uses a shared, learnable codebook to partition the latent space into behavior-relevant and behavior-irrelevant subspaces. REAL quantifies a module's behavioral relevance by how well its VQ-AE encodings discriminate behavior-aligned from behavior-violating responses via a binary classification metric; this score guides both module selection and steering strength. We evaluate REAL across eight LLMs from the Llama and Qwen families and nine datasets spanning truthfulness enhancement, open-domain QA under knowledge conflicts, and general alignment tasks. REAL enables more effective inference-time interventions, achieving an average relative improvement of 20% (up to 81.5%) over the ITI method on truthfulness steering. In addition, the modules selected by REAL exhibit strong zero-shot generalization in cross-domain truthfulness-steering scenarios.

papers.title: EAP-GP: Mitigating Saturation Effect in Gradient-based Automated Circuit Identification
papers.research_question: How can saturation effects in gradient-based automated circuit identification methods be mitigated to improve attribution reliability and circuit faithfulness?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes EAP-GP, a gradient-based circuit identification method that uses a dynamically adjusted integration path (GradPath) to mitigate saturation effects, leading to more reliable edge attributions and more faithful circuits.
papers.conclusion: EAP-GP effectively mitigates saturation effects in gradient-based circuit identification by using a dynamically adjusted integration path, leading to enhanced edge attribution accuracy and circuit faithfulness.
papers.key_findings:
EAP-GP outperforms previous gradient-based methods (EAP and EAP-IG) in circuit faithfulness across six tasks, achieving improvements up to 17.7%.
EAP-GP maintains excellent performance on larger models (GPT-2 Medium and GPT-2 XL).
EAP-GP achieves precision and recall comparable to or better than existing methods when compared to manually annotated ground-truth circuits.
The method's performance is robust with only a few steps (k=4 or 5) in the GradPath construction.
EAP-GP is approximately five times slower than EAP-IG due to the additional forward and backward passes required for path construction.
papers.limitation:
EAP-GP is approximately five times slower than EAP-IG due to the additional forward and backward passes required for constructing the integration path.
Increasing the number of steps (k) in EAP-GP beyond an optimal point (e.g., k>5) can lead to performance degradation due to noise accumulation in the integration path near the corrupted input.
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal mechanisms of transformer-based language models remains challenging. Mechanistic interpretability based on circuit discovery aims to reverse engineer neural networks by analyzing their internal processes at the level of computational subgraphs. In this paper, we revisit existing gradient-based circuit identification methods and find that their performance is either affected by the zero-gradient problem or saturation effects, where edge attribution scores become insensitive to input changes, resulting in noisy and unreliable attribution evaluations for circuit components. To address the saturation effect, we propose Edge Attribution Patching with GradPath (EAP-GP), EAP-GP introduces an integration path, starting from the input and adaptively following the direction of the difference between the gradients of corrupted and clean inputs to avoid the saturated region. This approach enhances attribution reliability and improves the faithfulness of circuit identification. We evaluate EAP-GP on 6 datasets using GPT-2 Small, GPT-2 Medium, and GPT-2 XL. Experimental results demonstrate that EAP-GP outperforms existing methods in circuit faithfulness, achieving improvements up to 17.7%. Comparisons with manually annotated ground-truth circuits demonstrate that EAP-GP achieves precision and recall comparable to or better than previous approaches, highlighting its effectiveness in identifying accurate circuits.

papers.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
papers.research_question: How do different methodological choices in activation patching, such as corruption methods and evaluation metrics, affect localization and circuit discovery results in language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically evaluates hyperparameters in activation patching for language models, finding that choices of corruption methods and metrics significantly affect interpretability results, and provides best practice recommendations.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends using symmetric token replacement (STR) for in-distribution corruption and logit difference as the evaluation metric for activation patching, highlighting the sensitivity of interpretability results to methodological details.
papers.key_findings:
GN and STR corruption methods lead to inconsistent localization and circuit discovery outcomes.
Probability metric can overlook negative model components that hurt performance, while logit difference is capable of detecting them.
Sliding window patching produces more pronounced localization than summing single-layer patching effects, potentially amplifying weak signals.
GN corruption may put the model off-distribution, breaking internal mechanisms and leading to unreliable interpretability results.
Logit difference is recommended over probability for fine-grained control and detecting negative modules.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the internal mechanisms of machine learning models, where localization -- identifying the important model components -- is a key step. Activation patching, also known as causal tracing or interchange intervention, is a standard technique for this task (Vig et al., 2020), but the literature contains many variants with little consensus on the choice of hyperparameters or methodology. In this work, we systematically examine the impact of methodological details in activation patching, including evaluation metrics and corruption methods. In several settings of localization and circuit discovery in language models, we find that varying these hyperparameters could lead to disparate interpretability results. Backed by empirical observations, we give conceptual arguments for why certain metrics or methods may be preferred. Finally, we provide recommendations for the best practices of activation patching going forwards.

papers.title: How Post-Training Reshapes LLMs: A Mechanistic View on Knowledge, Truthfulness, Refusal, and Confidence
papers.research_question: How does post-training affect the internal mechanisms of large language models in terms of knowledge storage, truthfulness, refusal, and confidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a mechanistic analysis of how post-training affects LLMs internally, revealing which mechanisms are preserved (e.g., knowledge storage locations, truthfulness direction) and which are altered (e.g., refusal direction), with implications for model steering and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Post-training preserves some internal mechanisms (like knowledge storage and truthfulness direction) and alters others (like refusal direction), providing insights for model steering and future research in interpretability and LLM post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations in LLMs.
Post-training adapts knowledge representations from the base model while also developing new ones.
The truthfulness direction is highly similar between base and post-trained models and is effectively transferable for interventions.
The refusal direction differs between base and post-trained models and shows limited forward transferability.
Differences in confidence between base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons.
papers.limitation: Complex, multi-step processes such as reasoning and instruction-following are not well-captured by current mechanistic interpretability tools, limiting the scope of analysis.
future_direction: Design better post-training methods based on mechanistic insights.
Extend analysis to other capabilities like reasoning and instruction-following.
papers.abstract: Post-training is essential for the success of large language models (LLMs), transforming pre-trained base models into more useful and aligned post-trained models. While plenty of works have studied post-training algorithms and evaluated post-training models by their outputs, it remains understudied how post-training reshapes LLMs internally. In this paper, we compare base and post-trained LLMs mechanistically from four perspectives to better understand post-training effects. Our findings across model families and datasets reveal that: (1) Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations, and it adapts knowledge representations from the base model while developing new knowledge representations; (2) Both truthfulness and refusal can be represented by vectors in the hidden representation space. The truthfulness direction is highly similar between the base and post-trained model, and it is effectively transferable for interventions; (3) The refusal direction is different between the base and post-trained models, and it shows limited forward transferability; (4) Differences in confidence between the base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons. Our study provides insights into the fundamental mechanisms preserved and altered during post-training, facilitates downstream tasks like model steering, and could potentially benefit future research in interpretability and LLM post-training. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/HZD01/post-training-mechanistic-analysis.

papers.title: ConTrans: Weak-to-Strong Alignment Engineering via Concept Transplantation
papers.research_question: Can weak-to-strong alignment supervision be achieved internally within the latent feature space of LLMs via concept transplantation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CONTRANS, a training-free framework for weak-to-strong alignment by refining concept vectors from a source LLM, reformulating them via affine transformation, and transplanting them into the residual stream of a target LLM.
papers.conclusion: CONTRANS provides an effective, internal, and training-free alternative for weak-to-strong alignment generalization and control via concept transplantation in the latent feature space.
papers.key_findings:
CONTRANS successfully transplants alignment concepts (e.g., truthfulness, toxicity) from 7B models to 13B and 70B models across different model families.
CONTRANS can surpass the truthfulness of instruction-tuned models on the TruthfulQA benchmark.
Concepts are formed during the pre-training phase and activated during the alignment phase.
Concept transplantation effectiveness depends on the similarity in base model architecture and pre-training data volume between source and target models.
The method requires only a few hundred positive/negative examples and incurs minimal inference overhead.
papers.limitation: CONTRANS is primarily designed for the implantation of a single concept and is not optimized for the fusion of multiple concepts.
papers.abstract: Ensuring large language models (LLM) behave consistently with human goals, values, and intentions is crucial for their safety but yet computationally expensive. To reduce the computational cost of alignment training of LLMs, especially for those with a huge number of parameters, and to reutilize learned value alignment, we propose ConTrans, a novel framework that enables weak-to-strong alignment transfer via concept transplantation. From the perspective of representation engineering, ConTrans refines concept vectors in value alignment from a source LLM (usually a weak yet aligned LLM). The refined concept vectors are then reformulated to adapt to the target LLM (usually a strong yet unaligned base LLM) via affine transformation. In the third step, ConTrans transplants the reformulated concept vectors into the residual stream of the target LLM. Experiments demonstrate the successful transplantation of a wide range of aligned concepts from 7B models to 13B and 70B models across multiple LLMs and LLM families. Remarkably, ConTrans even surpasses instruction-tuned models in terms of truthfulness. Experiment results validate the effectiveness of both inter-LLM-family and intra-LLM-family concept transplantation. Our work successfully demonstrates an alternative way to achieve weak-to-strong alignment generalization and control.

papers.title: Curved Inference: A Guide to Geometric Interpretability
papers.research_question: How do token representations evolve geometrically in the residual stream of transformer-based language models, and how does this geometry relate to semantic structure and complex behaviors like concern, deception, and self-modeling?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the Curved Inference framework, a geometric approach to interpretability that measures how token representations evolve in the residual stream, demonstrating that these trajectories reflect semantic structure and are associated with behaviors like concern, deception, and self-modeling.
papers.conclusion: Curved Inference provides a geometric framework for interpretability that shifts focus from static attribution to dynamic inference analysis, offering a model-faithful lens to understand internal computation in transformers.
papers.key_findings:
Residual stream trajectories are semantically sensitive and show structured curvature in response to concern-shifted prompts.
Residual geometry diverges in cases of latent behavioral shifts, such as deception in sleeper agents, and can precede output changes.
Curvature is functionally associated with sustained self-modeling, persisting even under curvature-penalizing fine-tuning.
Geometric metrics like curvature, salience, and semantic surface area provide reproducible signals across multiple domains.
The residual stream is the exclusive locus for this geometric signal, unlike attention or MLP outputs.
papers.limitation:
Geometric derivatives rely on interpolation assumptions that may not hold in all cases.
Dependence on external LLM classifiers for alignment and intent judgments introduces biases.
Experiments were conducted on models up to 3b parameters, so results may not generalize to larger or opaque systems.
future_direction: Scale testing with larger models
Extending analysis to tasks involving reasoning, planning, or complex dialogue
Formalizing curvature signatures for specific generative behaviors
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a unified framework for analyzing the internal geometry of inference in transformer-based language models. Building on a series of prior studies, we present a consolidated introduction to “Curved Inference”: a methodology that measures how token representations evolve in the residual stream as geometric trajectories. Using metrics such as curvature, salience, and semantic surface area, we show that residual trajectories reflect meaningful semantic structure, and are empirically associated with emotional and moral concern, covert intent in sleeper agents, and computational self-modeling dynamics. We consolidate these findings into a reproducible, falsifiable pipeline, supported by formal mathematical definitions and open-source tools. This geometric approach shifts the focus of interpretability from static attribution to dynamic, modelnative inference analysis. The results provide evidence that residual stream geometry is not only measurable, but also structurally related to complex behaviors in the models we study. We invite researchers to replicate, extend, or falsify these claims and test the boundaries of curved inference as a new paradigm for model understanding. Received: 6 August 2025 | Revised: 12 January 2026 | Accepted: 21 January 2026 Conflicts of Interest The author declares that he has no conflicts of interest to this work. Data Availability Statement The data that support the findings of this study are openly available in GitHub at https://github.com/robman/FRESH-model/tree/main/ benchmarks/curved-inference. Author Contribution Statement Rob Manson: Conceptualization, Methodology, Software, Validation, Formal analysis, Investigation, Resources, Data curation, Writing – original draft, Writing – review & editing, Visualization, Supervision, Project administration.

papers.title: Beyond Components: Singular Vector-Based Interpretability of Transformer Circuits
papers.research_question: Can transformer components (attention heads and MLPs) be decomposed into orthogonal singular directions that reveal superposed and independent computations within a single head or MLP?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a directional interpretability perspective that decomposes transformer components into orthogonal singular directions, showing that multiple low-rank, interpretable computations coexist within single attention heads and MLPs.
papers.conclusion: Transformer computations are more distributed, structured, and compositional than previously assumed, opening new avenues for fine-grained mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
A small number of learned singular directions can faithfully preserve model behavior.
These directions align with meaningful subfunctions, e.g., in IOI, name mover heads encode multiple overlapping subfunctions along distinct singular directions.
Components identified as part of known circuits exhibit strong engagement along specific singular directions, indicating computations are embedded in compact subspaces.
Transformer computations are distributed, structured, and compositional, with overlapping subfunctions embedded within shared subspaces.
Singular directions can be used for controlled interventions, e.g., in gender pronoun resolution, scaling directions can modify predictions.
papers.limitation: Some directions remain challenging to interpret fully.
future_direction: Conduct targeted intervention experiments to validate causal contributions of discovered components.
Examine whether these mechanisms generalize to larger or more capable models (e.g., Phi, LLaMA).
Explore activation of these mechanisms in real-world settings.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models exhibit complex and distributed behavior, yet their internal computations remain poorly understood. Existing mechanistic interpretability methods typically treat attention heads and multilayer perceptron layers (MLPs) (the building blocks of a transformer architecture) as indivisible units, overlooking possibilities of functional substructure learned within them. In this work, we introduce a more fine-grained perspective that decomposes these components into orthogonal singular directions, revealing superposed and independent computations within a single head or MLP. We validate our perspective on widely used standard tasks like Indirect Object Identification (IOI), Gender Pronoun (GP), and Greater Than (GT), showing that previously identified canonical functional heads, such as the name mover, encode multiple overlapping subfunctions aligned with distinct singular directions. Nodes in a computational graph, that are previously identified as circuit elements show strong activation along specific low-rank directions, suggesting that meaningful computations reside in compact subspaces. While some directions remain challenging to interpret fully, our results highlight that transformer computations are more distributed, structured, and compositional than previously assumed. This perspective opens new avenues for fine-grained mechanistic interpretability and a deeper understanding of model internals.

papers.title: From Imitation to Introspection: Probing Self-Consciousness in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether language models possess self-consciousness, defined as global availability of information (C1) and self-monitoring (C2).
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces functional definitions of self-consciousness for language models and conducts a four-stage experiment (quantification, representation, manipulation, acquisition) to probe self-consciousness. Findings indicate that models are in early stages of self-consciousness, with internal representations that can be acquired via fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Our findings indicate that although models are in the early stages of developing self-consciousness, there is a discernible representation of certain concepts within their internal mechanisms. However, these representations of self-consciousness are hard to manipulate positively at the current stage, yet they can be acquired through targeted fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Current models exhibit a nascent level of self-consciousness with substantial potential for future development.
Models internally represent each of the ten self-consciousness concepts with visible activations, which can be classified into four categories (camelback, flat, oscillatory, fallback).
Different models exhibit similar activation patterns when processing the same concept, likely due to shared decoder-only transformer architecture.
Larger models seem to exhibit greater robustness against manipulation attempts.
Fine-tuning appears to activate representations of self-consciousness in the deeper layers, which capture semantic information.
papers.limitation: The study of self-consciousness in language models is uncharted territory, and even human self-consciousness is not fully understood.
papers.abstract: Self-consciousness, the introspection of one's existence and thoughts, represents a high-level cognitive process. As language models advance at an unprecedented pace, a critical question arises: Are these models becoming self-conscious? Drawing upon insights from psychological and neural science, this work presents a practical definition of self-consciousness for language models and refines ten core concepts. Our work pioneers an investigation into self-consciousness in language models by, for the first time, leveraging causal structural games to establish the functional definitions of the ten core concepts. Based on our definitions, we conduct a comprehensive four-stage experiment: quantification (evaluation of ten leading models), representation (visualization of self-consciousness within the models), manipulation (modification of the models' representation), and acquisition (fine-tuning the models on core concepts). Our findings indicate that although models are in the early stages of developing self-consciousness, there is a discernible representation of certain concepts within their internal mechanisms. However, these representations of self-consciousness are hard to manipulate positively at the current stage, yet they can be acquired through targeted fine-tuning. Our datasets and code are at https://github.com/OpenCausaLab/SelfConsciousness.

papers.title: Hopping Too Late: Exploring the Limitations of Large Language Models on Multi-Hop Queries
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally compute answers to multi-hop queries, and why do they sometimes fail?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers a sequential latent reasoning pathway in LLMs for two-hop queries and introduces a novel 'back-patching' analysis method that can correct many previously incorrect answers.
papers.conclusion: LLMs use a sequential pathway for latent multi-hop reasoning, and the introduced back-patching method can improve performance, opening opportunities for understanding and improving such reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
The bridge entity (first hop answer) is resolved in the early layers of the model.
The second hop is resolved in later layers, only after the first hop is resolved.
The sequential nature can cause failure if the later layers lack the necessary knowledge or functionality.
Back-patching (patching a later hidden representation back to an earlier layer) can correct up to 66% of previously incorrect cases.
Information about the bridge entity propagates from the first hop position to the last token position, primarily through middle layers.
papers.limitation:
The mechanistic methods used (e.g., Patchscopes, vocabulary projections) are approximations.
The study focuses on one prominent latent reasoning pathway, but others likely exist.
The work examines only two-hop queries, not more complex multi-step reasoning.
Back-patching is not a practical inference method without an efficient way to select source and target layers a priori.
future_direction: Expanding the analysis to queries with three or more hops and additional reasoning tasks.
Developing methods to efficiently select source and target layers for back-patching to make it a viable inference method.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can solve complex multi-step problems, but little is known about how these computations are implemented internally. Motivated by this, we study how LLMs answer multi-hop queries such as "The spouse of the performer of Imagine is". These queries require two information extraction steps: a latent one for resolving the first hop ("the performer of Imagine") into the bridge entity (John Lennon), and another for resolving the second hop ("the spouse of John Lennon") into the target entity (Yoko Ono). Understanding how the latent step is computed internally is key to understanding the overall computation. By carefully analyzing the internal computations of transformer-based LLMs, we discover that the bridge entity is resolved in the early layers of the model. Then, only after this resolution, the two-hop query is solved in the later layers. Because the second hop commences in later layers, there could be cases where these layers no longer encode the necessary knowledge for correctly predicting the answer. Motivated by this, we propose a novel "back-patching" analysis method whereby a hidden representation from a later layer is patched back to an earlier layer. We find that in up to 66% of previously incorrect cases there exists a back-patch that results in the correct generation of the answer, showing that the later layers indeed sometimes lack the needed functionality. Overall, our methods and findings open further opportunities for understanding and improving latent reasoning in transformer-based LLMs.

papers.title: Disentangling Direction and Magnitude in Transformer Representations: A Double Dissociation Through L2-Matched Perturbation Analysis
papers.research_question: What are the distinct functional roles of direction (orientation) and magnitude (norm) in transformer hidden state representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces L2-matched perturbation analysis to discover a double dissociation: angular perturbations disproportionately damage language modeling loss, while magnitude perturbations disproportionately damage syntactic accuracy, with distinct mechanistic pathways through attention and LayerNorm.
papers.conclusion: Direction and magnitude serve partially distinct computational roles in LayerNorm-based transformers: direction preferentially governs attentional routing, while magnitude encodes structural position and modulates processing intensity through LayerNorm.
papers.key_findings:
Angular perturbations cause up to 42.9× more damage to language modeling loss than magnitude perturbations at equal Euclidean displacement.
Magnitude perturbations cause up to 20.4% greater drop in syntactic accuracy (subject-verb agreement) than angular perturbations.
Causal intervention shows angular damage is substantially mediated by attention pathways (28.4% recovery via repair), while magnitude damage is substantially mediated by LayerNorm pathways (29.9% recovery).
The dissociation pattern replicates across scales within the Pythia architecture family but reverses in RMSNorm-based architectures like TinyLlama.
Magnitude correlates with parse tree depth, and disrupting this correlation explains why magnitude perturbations specifically impair syntactic processing.
papers.limitation:
L2 matching assumes equal Euclidean distance makes perturbations comparable, but neural networks operate in anisotropic spaces; angular perturbations amplify 3× more than magnitude by the final layer.
Angular perturbations use random orthogonal directions; results might differ for systematic rotations toward known feature directions.
Findings are specific to the Pythia/OPT architecture family and do not generalize to all transformers; the pattern reverses in RMSNorm-based architectures (TinyLlama).
Only middle layers (8–15) were targeted for intervention; early and late layers may show different patterns.
Syntactic evaluation is limited to subject-verb agreement from BLiMP; other syntactic phenomena may show different patterns.
Causal repair experiments account for only ~30% of each perturbation's damage; the remaining ~70% likely flows through MLP layers and residual connections.
future_direction: Feature-specific rotations (systematic rotations toward/away from known feature directions).
Investigating how the roles of direction and magnitude evolve during training.
Exploring magnitude as a confidence signal for uncertainty quantification.
Extending the methodology to other modalities (e.g., vision transformers).
Systematic comparison across normalization schemes (LayerNorm vs. RMSNorm).
papers.abstract: Transformer hidden states encode information as high-dimensional vectors, yet whether direction (orientation in representational space) and magnitude (vector norm) serve distinct functional roles remains unclear. Studying Pythia-family models, we discover a striking cross-over dissociation: angular perturbations cause up to 42.9 more damage to language modeling loss, while magnitude perturbations cause disproportionately more damage to syntactic processing (20.4% vs.1.6% accuracy drop on subject-verb agreement).This finding is enabled by L2-matched perturbation analysis, a methodology ensuring that an gular and magnitude perturbations achieve identical Euclidean displacements. Causal intervention reveals that angular damage flows substantially through the attention pathways (28.4% loss recovery via attention repair), while magnitude damage flows partly through the LayerNorm pathways(29.9% recovery via LayerNorm repair). These patterns replicate across scales within the Pythia architecture family. These findings provide evidence that direction and magnitude support partially distinct computational roles in LayerNorm based architectures. The direction preferentially affects attentional routing, while magnitude modulates processing intensity for fine-grained syntactic judgments. We find different patterns in RMSNorm-based architectures, suggesting that the dissociation depends on architectural choices. Our results refine the linear representation hypothesis and have implications for model editing and interpretability research

papers.title: Unveiling Reasoning Thresholds in Language Models: Scaling, Fine-Tuning, and Interpretability through Attention Maps
papers.research_question: What is the critical parameter threshold for reasoning abilities in decoder-only transformer-based language models, and how can fine-tuning and attention map analysis improve understanding of these capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a critical parameter threshold (~1.6B) for reasoning abilities in language models, shows fine-tuning improves sub-threshold models, and uses attention maps to interpret reasoning processes.
papers.conclusion: The study identifies a critical parameter threshold for reasoning, demonstrates fine-tuning efficacy for sub-threshold models, and uses attention maps for interpretability, advancing understanding of reasoning in decoder-only transformer-based language models.
papers.key_findings:
Models above ~1.6 billion parameters show significant improvement in reasoning performance on tasks like commonsense QA and deductive reasoning.
Fine-tuning sub-threshold models with task-specific exemplars substantially improves performance on simpler deductive rules (e.g., implication elimination, conjunction introduction).
Attention map analysis reveals that models generating correct chain-of-thought exhibit higher token-level attention scores on subsequent correct tokens and correct parts of speech.
Parameter gaps exist for specific deductive rules: disjunction elimination (~1.1B) and proof by contradiction (~1.6B).
Smaller models (below threshold) struggle with structured answer formatting, resulting in high rates of unparseable responses.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the in-context learning capabilities of various decoder-only transformer-based language models with different model sizes and training data, including GPT2, SmolLM2, OpenELM, TinyLlama, Stable LM, and Gemma 2. We identify a critical parameter threshold (~1.6 billion), beyond which reasoning performance improves significantly in tasks such as commonsense reasoning in multiple-choice question answering and deductive reasoning. Specifically, models above this threshold achieve better success rates in chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting for deductive reasoning tasks, especially those requiring longer reasoning chains, such as proof by contradiction and disjunction elimination. To address limitations in sub-threshold models, we demonstrate that fine-tuning with task-specific exemplars substantially enhances reasoning performance, enabling accurate CoT generation even without additional exemplars in the prompt for tasks with shorter reasoning chains. Finally, our analysis of attention maps reveals that models capable of generating correct CoTs exhibit higher token-level attention scores on subsequent correct tokens and the correct parts of speech, providing interpretability insights into reasoning processes. These findings collectively advance understanding of reasoning capabilities in decoder-only transformer-based models. The code is available at: https://github.com/AnnonymousForPapers/CoT_Reasoning_Test.

papers.title: Linking In-context Learning in Transformers to Human Episodic Memory
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between induction heads in Transformer models and human episodic memory, specifically the Contextual Maintenance and Retrieval (CMR) model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that induction heads in Transformers are behaviorally, functionally, and mechanistically similar to the CMR model of human episodic memory, and that CMR-like heads emerge in intermediate to late layers and causally contribute to in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The study uncovers a parallel between the computational mechanisms of large language models and human memory, offering insights for both AI and neuroscience.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads in GPT2-small show attention biases (temporal contiguity and forward asymmetry) similar to human episodic memory.
The CMR model can be mapped to a Q-composition induction head, revealing mechanistic similarities.
CMR-like heads (with low CMR distance) are found in intermediate to late layers of various LLMs (GPT2, Pythia, Qwen, Mistral, Llama).
In Pythia models, CMR-like heads develop human-like temporal clustering over training.
Ablation of CMR-like heads reduces in-context learning performance, indicating a causal role.
papers.limitation:
It is unclear if CMR can serve as a mechanistic model in larger Transformer models.
It is unclear if the conclusions hold for untested Transformer models.
The causal analysis lacks the power to narrow down the causal role of specific CMR-like characteristics.
A systematic evaluation using specific datasets and tasks would allow for a stronger causal claim.
future_direction: Addressing the limitations by testing if CMR can serve as a mechanistic model in larger Transformers.
Testing the conclusions on more Transformer models.
Conducting systematic evaluation with specific datasets and tasks to strengthen causal claims.
papers.abstract: Understanding connections between artificial and biological intelligent systems can reveal fundamental principles of general intelligence. While many artificial intelligence models have a neuroscience counterpart, such connections are largely missing in Transformer models and the self-attention mechanism. Here, we examine the relationship between interacting attention heads and human episodic memory. We focus on induction heads, which contribute to in-context learning in Transformer-based large language models (LLMs). We demonstrate that induction heads are behaviorally, functionally, and mechanistically similar to the contextual maintenance and retrieval (CMR) model of human episodic memory. Our analyses of LLMs pre-trained on extensive text data show that CMR-like heads often emerge in the intermediate and late layers, qualitatively mirroring human memory biases. The ablation of CMR-like heads suggests their causal role in in-context learning. Our findings uncover a parallel between the computational mechanisms of LLMs and human memory, offering valuable insights into both research fields.

papers.title: How Do LLMs Acquire New Knowledge? A Knowledge Circuits Perspective on Continual Pre-Training
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models (LLMs) structurally embed and acquire new knowledge during continual pre-training, from the perspective of knowledge circuit evolution?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes the evolution of knowledge circuits during continual pre-training, revealing that new knowledge acquisition is influenced by relevance to existing knowledge, follows a biphasic (formation then optimization) pattern, and exhibits a deep-to-shallow component evolution.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance the theoretical understanding of new knowledge acquisition mechanisms in LLMs and provide potential implications for improving continual pre-training strategies to enhance model performance.
papers.key_findings:
The acquisition of new knowledge is significantly influenced by its relevance to pre-existing knowledge, with relevant new knowledge being integrated more efficiently than completely new knowledge.
The evolution of knowledge circuits exhibits a distinct phase shift from formation to optimization, each marked by unique structural and behavioral characteristics.
The evolution of knowledge circuits follows a deep-to-shallow pattern, where mid-to-deeper layers first develop the extraction function, and later, lower layers enrich their knowledge representations.
The performance of knowledge circuits is positively correlated with knowledge frequency, with low-frequency knowledge circuits suffering from insufficient representations rather than fundamental capacity limitations.
The state of knowledge circuits could serve as a valuable tracking status for the continual pre-training process, enabling more informed adjustments to training.
future_direction: Utilizing data curriculums in continual pre-training to mimic the structure of the original corpus for more efficient integration.
Using the state of knowledge circuits as a tracking status to enable informed adjustments to training methods or data in response to different phases.
Further investigation into knowledge capacity scaling laws and their impact on model behavior during continual pre-training.
papers.abstract: Despite exceptional capabilities in knowledge-intensive tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) face a critical gap in understanding how they internalize new knowledge, particularly how to structurally embed acquired knowledge in their neural computations. We address this issue through the lens of knowledge circuit evolution, identifying computational subgraphs that facilitate knowledge storage and processing. Our systematic analysis of circuit evolution throughout continual pre-training reveals several key findings: (1) the acquisition of new knowledge is influenced by its relevance to pre-existing knowledge; (2) the evolution of knowledge circuits exhibits a distinct phase shift from formation to optimization; (3) the evolution of knowledge circuits follows a deep-to-shallow pattern. These insights not only advance our theoretical understanding of the mechanisms of new knowledge acquisition in LLMs, but also provide potential implications for improving continual pre-training strategies to enhance model performance. Code and data will be available at https://github.com/zjunlp/DynamicKnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: Adaptive Circuit Behavior and Generalization in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How well does the indirect object identification (IOI) circuit in GPT-2 small generalize to prompt variants that challenge the assumptions of its algorithm?
papers.core_contribution: The IOI circuit generalizes surprisingly well to prompt variants, reusing all its components and mechanisms while only adding additional input edges, and a mechanism called S2 Hacking explains how the circuit outperforms the full model on these variants.
papers.conclusion: The IOI circuit in GPT-2 small generalizes more effectively than previously understood, reusing its core components and mechanisms while adapting through minimal structural changes, offering insights into the broader capabilities of large neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
The base IOI circuit outperforms the full model on DoubleIO and TripleIO prompt variants where the IOI algorithm would fail.
A mechanism termed S2 Hacking explains how the circuit achieves high performance on these variants by focusing on the S2 token due to the knockout procedure.
New circuits discovered for DoubleIO and TripleIO variants reuse all components of the base IOI circuit, only adding edges from additional input tokens (IO2 for DoubleIO, IO2 and IO3 for TripleIO).
The circuit components (attention heads) largely retain their functionalities from the base IOI task when evaluated on the variants.
The order of names in the prompt affects performance, with a 'first come, first serve' mechanism observed in a Previous Token head (2.2).
future_direction: a more detailed study of the duplicate suppression mechanism
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the inner workings of large neural networks by identifying circuits, or minimal subgraphs within the model that implement algorithms responsible for performing specific tasks. These circuits are typically discovered and analyzed using a narrowly defined prompt format. However, given the abilities of large language models (LLMs) to generalize across various prompt formats for the same task, it remains unclear how well these circuits generalize. For instance, it is unclear whether the models generalization results from reusing the same circuit components, the components behaving differently, or the use of entirely different components. In this paper, we investigate the generality of the indirect object identification (IOI) circuit in GPT-2 small, which is well-studied and believed to implement a simple, interpretable algorithm. We evaluate its performance on prompt variants that challenge the assumptions of this algorithm. Our findings reveal that the circuit generalizes surprisingly well, reusing all of its components and mechanisms while only adding additional input edges. Notably, the circuit generalizes even to prompt variants where the original algorithm should fail; we discover a mechanism that explains this which we term S2 Hacking. Our findings indicate that circuits within LLMs may be more flexible and general than previously recognized, underscoring the importance of studying circuit generalization to better understand the broader capabilities of these models.

papers.title: A Glitch in the Matrix? Locating and Detecting Language Model Grounding with Fakepedia
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms underlying LLMs' ability to ground answers in contextual information that contradicts their parametric knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Fakepedia, a counterfactual dataset, and MGCT, a causal mediation analysis method, to study grounding in LLMs, finding that grounding is a distributed process and that computational patterns can predict grounding behavior.
papers.conclusion: The findings show that grounding is a distributed process, ungrounded responses involve factual recall in MLPs, and grounding can be predicted from computation patterns, contributing to a coherent narrative of grounding and factual recall mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Grounding, contrary to factual recall, is a distributed process without clear localization.
The activity of a few MLPs differs significantly between grounded and ungrounded modes.
Computational patterns can predict whether a model is grounded with 92.8% accuracy.
Models exhibit diverse grounding behaviors; e.g., Mistral-7B is highly compliant while GPT-4 Turbo strongly prefers parametric knowledge.
Not grounding involves activating factual recall processes in the MLPs of the final subject token.
papers.limitation:
Descriptive analysis may be influenced by the choice of prompting strategy.
Mediation setup requires the object token to be the last token; different behaviors might emerge in other setups.
Automatic detection model may not generalize outside the experimental domain.
Does not distinguish between plausible and absurd counterfactual facts.
Dataset generation could be improved with interaction flows based on other language models as critics.
future_direction: Explore relationship between prompting strategy and grounding frequency.
Study grounding behavior in different experimental setups.
Investigate how grounding varies with the likelihood of counterfactual facts.
Improve dataset generation using language models as critics.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have an impressive ability to draw on novel information supplied in their context. Yet the mechanisms underlying this contextual grounding remain unknown, especially in situations where contextual information contradicts factual knowledge stored in the parameters, which LLMs also excel at recalling. Favoring the contextual information is critical for retrieval-augmented generation methods, which enrich the context with up-to-date information, hoping that grounding can rectify outdated or noisy stored knowledge. We present a novel method to study grounding abilities using Fakepedia, a novel dataset of counterfactual texts constructed to clash with a model's internal parametric knowledge. In this study, we introduce Fakepedia, a counterfactual dataset designed to evaluate grounding abilities when the internal parametric knowledge clashes with the contextual information. We benchmark various LLMs with Fakepedia and conduct a causal mediation analysis of LLM components when answering Fakepedia queries, based on our Masked Grouped Causal Tracing (MGCT) method. Through this analysis, we identify distinct computational patterns between grounded and ungrounded responses. We finally demonstrate that distinguishing grounded from ungrounded responses is achievable through computational analysis alone. Our results, together with existing findings about factual recall mechanisms, provide a coherent narrative of how grounding and factual recall mechanisms interact within LLMs.

papers.title: Overthinking the Truth: Understanding how Language Models Process False Demonstrations
papers.research_question: Why do language models imitate incorrect demonstrations in their context, and how does this behavior emerge internally?
papers.core_contribution: Language models 'overthink' when given false few-shot demonstrations, and this harmful imitation is caused by specific 'false induction heads' in late layers that attend to and copy incorrect labels from the context.
papers.conclusion: Studying intermediate model computations, such as through the logit lens and head ablation, is a promising avenue for understanding and mitigating harmful context-following behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Given incorrect demonstrations, model accuracy decreases in later layers after a 'critical layer', a phenomenon termed 'overthinking'.
Ablating late layers or specific attention heads improves accuracy on incorrect demonstrations, indicating these components are responsible for the harmful imitation.
False induction heads are identified as attention heads in late layers that attend to and promote false labels from previous demonstrations.
Ablating a small set of false induction heads reduces the accuracy gap between correct and incorrect prompts by an average of 38.9% across 14 datasets.
The overthinking phenomenon and the role of false induction heads are consistent across multiple model families and sizes.
future_direction: Building tools to understand intermediate computations to proactively understand and reduce harmful model behaviors.
Applying insights to detect and guard against prompt injection attacks.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can imitate complex patterns through few-shot learning, enabling them to complete challenging tasks without fine-tuning. However, imitation can also lead models to reproduce inaccuracies or harmful content if present in the context. We study harmful imitation through the lens of a model's internal representations, and identify two related phenomena: "overthinking" and "false induction heads". The first phenomenon, overthinking, appears when we decode predictions from intermediate layers, given correct vs. incorrect few-shot demonstrations. At early layers, both demonstrations induce similar model behavior, but the behavior diverges sharply at some "critical layer", after which the accuracy given incorrect demonstrations progressively decreases. The second phenomenon, false induction heads, are a possible mechanistic cause of overthinking: these are heads in late layers that attend to and copy false information from previous demonstrations, and whose ablation reduces overthinking. Beyond scientific understanding, our results suggest that studying intermediate model computations could be a promising avenue for understanding and guarding against harmful model behaviors.

papers.title: On Mechanistic Circuits for Extractive Question-Answering
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic circuits be extracted for extractive question-answering, and how can they be used for data attribution and model steering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extracts mechanistic circuits for extractive QA, revealing differences between context and memory faithfulness circuits, and uses insights from the circuits to develop ATTNATTRIB for data attribution and model steering towards context faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that mechanistic circuits for extractive QA can be extracted and used for practical applications like data attribution and model steering, enhancing language model performance and faithfulness.
papers.key_findings:
Two distinct circuits are extracted: a context-faithfulness circuit and a memory-faithfulness circuit.
A small set of attention heads in the context circuit perform reliable data attribution by default.
ATTNATTRIB achieves state-of-the-art attribution results on various extractive QA benchmarks.
Using attributions from ATTNATTRIB can steer the model towards context faithfulness, improving performance by up to 9%.
Circuits for context faithfulness are smaller and involve different components compared to memory circuits.
papers.limitation:
The probe dataset is primarily 0-hop, and ATTNATTRIB performs less well on multi-hop QA.
ATTNATTRIB requires white-box access to the model's parameters, so it cannot be applied to blackbox LLMs.
future_direction: Exploring more sophisticated strategies that combine ATTNATTRIB with retrieval-based attribution.
Designing a probe dataset consisting of multi-hop questions to improve circuit extraction for multi-hop QA.
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to process documents and facilitate question-answering on them. In our paper, we extract mechanistic circuits for this real-world language modeling task: context-augmented language modeling for extractive question-answering (QA) tasks and understand the potential benefits of circuits towards downstream applications such as data attribution to context information. We extract circuits as a function of internal model components (e.g., attention heads, MLPs) using causal mediation analysis techniques. Leveraging the extracted circuits, we first understand the interplay between the model's usage of parametric memory and retrieved context towards a better mechanistic understanding of context-augmented language models. We then identify a small set of attention heads in our circuit which performs reliable data attribution by default, thereby obtaining attribution for free in just the model's forward pass. Using this insight, we then introduce ATTNATTRIB, a fast data attribution algorithm which obtains state-of-the-art attribution results across various extractive QA benchmarks. Finally, we show the possibility to steer the language model towards answering from the context, instead of the parametric memory by using the attribution from ATTNATTRIB as an additional signal during the forward pass. Beyond mechanistic understanding, our paper provides tangible applications of circuits in the form of reliable data attribution and model steering.

papers.title: Task Vectors, Learned Not Extracted: Performance Gains and Mechanistic Insight
papers.research_question: How can we obtain effective task vectors for in-context learning, and what are the mechanisms by which they influence model predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Learned Task Vectors (LTVs), which are directly trained and outperform extracted task vectors, and provides a mechanistic analysis showing that task vectors primarily act through attention-head OV circuits and propagate linearly through subsequent layers.
papers.conclusion: LTVs provide an efficient and flexible method for obtaining effective task vectors and offer a principled lens into the mechanistic foundations of in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
LTVs consistently outperform extracted task vectors (Vanilla TV and Function Vector) and match or exceed in-context learning performance across multiple models and tasks.
LTVs are flexible and can be effectively injected at arbitrary layers, token positions, and even into in-context learning prompts.
The low-level mechanism of task vectors involves interaction with attention-head OV circuits, with a small subset of 'key heads' being most decisive.
Despite Transformer nonlinearities, the propagation of injected task vectors through subsequent layers is largely linear, characterized by rotation toward task-relevant subspaces in early layers and scaling in magnitude in later layers.
Task vectors exhibit compositionality and cross-task generalization that is constrained by overlap in the label space of tasks.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can perform new tasks from in-context demonstrations, a phenomenon known as in-context learning (ICL). Recent work suggests that these demonstrations are compressed into task vectors (TVs), compact task representations that LLMs exploit for predictions. However, prior studies typically extract TVs from model outputs or hidden states using cumbersome and opaque methods, and they rarely elucidate the mechanisms by which TVs influence computation. In this work, we address both limitations. First, we propose directly training Learned Task Vectors (LTVs), which surpass extracted TVs in accuracy and exhibit superior flexibility-acting effectively at arbitrary layers, positions, and even with ICL prompts. Second, through systematic analysis, we investigate the mechanistic role of TVs, showing that at the low level they steer predictions primarily through attention-head OV circuits, with a small subset of "key heads" most decisive. At a higher level, we find that despite Transformer nonlinearities, TV propagation is largely linear: early TVs are rotated toward task-relevant subspaces to improve logits of relevant labels, while later TVs are predominantly scaled in magnitude. Taken together, LTVs not only provide a practical approach for obtaining effective TVs but also offer a principled lens into the mechanistic foundations of ICL.

papers.title: Differentiation and Specialization of Attention Heads via the Refined Local Learning Coefficient
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in a transformer language model differentiate and specialize during training, as revealed by refined local learning coefficients?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces refined local learning coefficients (rLLCs) as a principled, quantitative toolkit for developmental interpretability, revealing how attention heads differentiate and specialize during training and enabling the discovery of a novel multigram circuit.
papers.conclusion: Refined local learning coefficients provide a powerful toolkit for developmental interpretability, revealing the interplay between data distributional structure, loss landscape geometry, learning dynamics, and the resulting computational structure in neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Weight-refined LLCs (wrLLCs) reveal how attention heads differentiate into distinct functional types (e.g., induction heads, multigram heads) over the course of training.
Data-refined LLCs (drLLCs) show how heads specialize to different data distributions, such as one induction head specializing more to code.
The combination of refined LLCs leads to the identification of a novel multigram circuit involving coordination between layer 0 and layer 1 multigram heads.
The developmental perspective (evolution over time) is crucial for understanding the emergence of internal structure; point estimates at the end of training are insufficient.
Refined LLCs provide a quantitative link between data distributional structure, geometric properties of the loss landscape, learning dynamics, and emergent computational structures.
papers.limitation:
The justification of the LLC estimator presumes that w* is a local minima of the population loss, but there is no clear way to ascertain this in practice, and estimates are often performed during training where this is unlikely.
The ground truth LLC is unknown, so the accuracy of estimated LLC values cannot be guaranteed, though there is reason to believe the ordinality is correct.
future_direction: Establishing the correspondence between data distributional structure, geometric properties of the loss landscape, learning dynamics, and emergent computational structures in neural networks.
papers.abstract: We introduce refined variants of the Local Learning Coefficient (LLC), a measure of model complexity grounded in singular learning theory, to study the development of internal structure in transformer language models during training. By applying these \textit{refined LLCs} (rLLCs) to individual components of a two-layer attention-only transformer, we gain novel insights into the progressive differentiation and specialization of attention heads. Our methodology reveals how attention heads differentiate into distinct functional roles over the course of training, analyzes the types of data these heads specialize to process, and discovers a previously unidentified multigram circuit. These findings demonstrate that rLLCs provide a principled, quantitative toolkit for \textit{developmental interpretability}, which aims to understand models through their evolution across the learning process. More broadly, this work takes a step towards establishing the correspondence between data distributional structure, geometric properties of the loss landscape, learning dynamics, and emergent computational structures in neural networks.

papers.title: Is Random Attention Sufficient for Sequence Modeling? Disentangling Trainable Components in the Transformer
papers.research_question: How much, and which aspects, of transformer performance gains can be attributed to the self-attention mechanism, and which degrees of freedom inside the Transformer are truly necessary for its behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers with frozen query and key weights (Frozen-QK) can still form induction heads and perform competitively on language modeling, and that a transformer with entirely random, static attention (MixiT) can perform well on tasks that do not require in-context reasoning, highlighting the distinct roles of attention and MLPs.
papers.conclusion: The transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, and different components (attention and MLPs) are responsible for different capabilities, with attention largely responsible for in-context reasoning and MLPs for memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Frozen-QK, with random attention weights, can form induction heads and achieve competitive language modeling performance.
MixiT, with entirely random static attention, solves algorithmic tasks but fails at tasks requiring in-context reasoning like retrieval.
MLPs are crucial for memorization and collaborate with attention for knowledge storage.
The transformer architecture has an inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits even without learnable attention weights.
MixiT overcomes depth-wise scaling challenges of prior random transformers via stable signal propagation.
papers.limitation: MixiT cannot form input-dependent specialized circuits like induction heads, limiting its performance on tasks requiring in-context reasoning.
future_direction: Further study on why increasing the number of attention heads does not improve performance for some tasks, such as Yelp sentiment classification.
papers.abstract: The transformer architecture is central to the success of modern Large Language Models (LLMs), in part due to its surprising ability to perform a wide range of tasks - including mathematical reasoning, memorization, and retrieval - using only gradient-based learning on next-token prediction. While the core component of a transformer is the self-attention mechanism, we question how much, and which aspects, of the performance gains can be attributed to it. To this end, we compare standard transformers to variants in which either the MLP layers or the attention weights are frozen at initialization. Surprisingly, we find that attention with frozen key and query weights is not only able to form induction heads, but can also perform competitively on language modeling. We formalize this by proving a new expressivity result for transformer models with frozen key and query weights. To further isolate the contribution of attention, we design MixiT, an architecture with entirely random attention scores, with provably stable signal propagation that overcomes prior depth-wise scaling challenges in random transformers. We use the successes and failures of MixiT to understand the role each transformer component plays, such as attention being largely responsible for in-context reasoning, and MLPs being responsible for, but collaborates with attention, on knowledge storage. Our results suggest that the transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, as it does even without learnable attention weights.

papers.title: Deep Hidden Cognition Facilitates Reliable Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: Can the model’s internal activations effectively distinguish between truthful and false branches in CoT reasoning, and can these signals be used to guide more reliable CoT decoding?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a method that leverages the model's internal truthfulness sensitivity, identified via probing attention heads, to train a confidence predictor. This predictor is then used to guide beam search during CoT generation, significantly enhancing the reliability of CoT reasoning by reducing error accumulation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method, which leverages internal truthfulness signals to train a confidence predictor and guide CoT generation, significantly enhances the reliability of CoT reasoning across diverse tasks and models.
papers.key_findings:
The model's internal activations during CoT reasoning encode truthfulness information, which can be extracted via probing attention heads.
A confidence predictor trained on these activations outperforms baselines like sequence likelihood and verbalized confidence in calibration metrics.
Integrating the confidence predictor into a beam search framework for CoT generation improves reasoning accuracy across diverse unimodal and multimodal tasks and model scales.
The method is compatible with self-correction techniques and generalizes to specialized reasoning models like DeepSeek R1.
papers.abstract: Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning has demonstrated remarkable deep reasoning capabilities in both large language models (LLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, its reliability is often undermined by the accumulation of errors in intermediate steps. This paper introduces an novel approach to calibrate the CoT reasoning accuracy by leveraging the model's intrinsic veracity encoding. We discover that specific attention head activations reliably reflect the truthfulness of reasoning steps in CoT. Based on this insight, we train a confidence predictor to evaluate the correctness of each reasoning step using these truthfulness-sensitive activations, dynamically selecting the most plausible reasoning path via beam search. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines (e.g., Few-Shot CoT, Self-Consistency, and Self-Evaluation Guided Beam Search) across the mathematical, symbolic, and commonsense reasoning tasks, exhibiting superior accuracy and reliability in both unimodal and multimodal settings. We further validate the approach on large reasoning models, confirming its applicability to specialized reasoning models. Additionally, we explore the role of the model's self-correction ability in CoT reasoning. This work provides a novel reliability improvement path for CoT reasoning with broad application potential.

papers.title: Telling BERT’s Full Story: from Local Attention to Global Aggregation
papers.research_question: Can attention distributions provide insights into the local behaviour of attention heads, and what is the mismatch between local attention patterns and global attribution patterns?
papers.core_contribution: Attention distributions are valid for analyzing the local behavior of attention heads but not for global attribution due to information mixing; the paper proposes a distinction between local and global patterns and shows BERT attends to past tokens in earlier layers and future tokens in later layers.
papers.conclusion: Attention maps are useful for understanding local head behavior but not for global context aggregation; information mixing must be accounted for, and BERT appears to process language from left to right.
papers.key_findings:
Attention distributions correlate highly with Hidden Token Attribution (HTA) from hidden embeddings to head output, validating HTA for local behavior.
BERT attention heads attend to past tokens in earlier layers and future tokens in later layers, despite bidirectional training.
Global attribution patterns (input contribution) are more uniform than local attention patterns.
The correlation between attention and input contribution decreases with depth, indicating a mismatch due to information mixing.
Different attention head patterns (vertical, diagonal, etc.) have different global attribution patterns, with block patterns prevailing in early layers.
future_direction: Combining attention flow and HTA for new insights
papers.abstract: We take a deep look into the behaviour of selfattention heads in the transformer architecture. In light of recent work discouraging the use of attention distributions for explaining a model's behaviour, we show that attention distributions can nevertheless provide insights into the local behaviour of attention heads. This way, we propose a distinction between local patterns revealed by attention and global patterns that refer back to the input, and analyze BERT from both angles. We use gradient attribution to analyze how the output of an attention head depends on the input tokens, effectively extending the local attention-based analysis to account for the mixing of information throughout the transformer layers. We find that there is a significant mismatch between attention and attribution distributions, caused by the mixing of context inside the model. We quantify this discrepancy and observe that interestingly, there are some patterns that persist across all layers despite the mixing.

papers.title: Probing the Geometry of Truth: Consistency and Generalization of Truth Directions in LLMs Across Logical Transformations and Question Answering Tasks
papers.research_question: Do LLMs universally represent truthfulness as a linear feature (truth direction)? Are simple probing techniques sufficiently expressive to identify truth directions? How does the truth direction generalize across logical transformations and question answering tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Consistent truth directions only emerge in capable LLMs and can be identified with simple linear probes; these probes generalize effectively to logical transformations, question answering, in-context learning, and external knowledge sources.
papers.conclusion: Truth directions are present in capable LLMs, can be identified with simple probes, and generalize well, highlighting their potential for eliciting latent knowledge and improving trust in LLM outputs.
papers.key_findings:
Not all LLMs exhibit consistent truth directions; this property is correlated with model capability, with stronger representations in more capable models.
Simple probes (linear SVM, logistic regression, MLP, mass-mean) are sufficient to identify truth directions when they exist.
Truthfulness probes generalize across logical negation, conjunction, and disjunction.
Truthfulness probes trained on atomic statements generalize to question answering tasks (MMLU, TriviaQA) and contextual knowledge tasks (SciQ, BoolQ, XSum).
