Transformers function as stochastic approximations of context-sensitive languages, which are widely recognized as models of human-like intelligence.
future_direction: Exploring expansions to general forms of context-sensitive grammars within autoregressive generation for improvements in performance and computational resource utilization.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), powered by Transformers, have demonstrated human-like intelligence capabilities, yet their underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. This paper presents a novel framework for interpreting LLMs as probabilistic left context-sensitive languages (CSLs) generators. We hypothesize that Transformers can be effectively decomposed into three fundamental components: context windows, attention mechanisms, and autoregressive generation frameworks. This decomposition allows for the development of more flexible and interpretable computational models, moving beyond the traditional view of attention and autoregression as inseparable processes. We argue that next-token predictions can be understood as probabilistic, dynamic approximations of left CSL production rules, providing an intuitive explanation for how simple token predictions can yield human-like intelligence outputs. Given that all CSLs are left context-sensitive (Penttonen, 1974), we conclude that Transformers stochastically approximate CSLs, which are widely recognized as models of human-like intelligence. This interpretation bridges the gap between Formal Language Theory and the observed generative power of Transformers, laying a foundation for future advancements in generative AI theory and applications. Our novel perspective on Transformer architectures will foster a deeper understanding of LLMs and their future potentials.

papers.title: Dissecting Persona-Driven Reasoning in Language Models via Activation Patching
papers.research_question: How does assigning a persona influence a language model's reasoning on objective tasks, and what internal mechanisms (circuits) are responsible for persona-driven behavior and potential social biases?
papers.core_contribution: Early MLP layers encode persona-specific semantic information, which is then used by middle MHA layers to influence reasoning; specific attention heads disproportionately attend to racial and color-based identities.
papers.conclusion: The work offers preliminary insight into the functions of certain model components and takes initial steps toward understanding the origins of persona-driven behavior in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Early MLP layers process semantic content and transform persona tokens into richer representations.
Middle MHA layers use these representations to shape the model's output.
Specific attention heads disproportionately attend to racial and color-based identities.
The effect of early MLP layers is indirect, via later layers.
Patching early MLP layers at the identity token position is nearly as effective as patching all positions.
papers.limitation:
The MMLU dataset is not the only dataset that meets the selection criteria.
Experiments were conducted on three models (Llama 1B, 3B, Qwen 1.5B) and head-level patching only on Llama 1B due to computational constraints.
The list of personas is not exhaustive.
Attention pattern analysis requires manual inspection, which is slow and labor-intensive.
future_direction: Investigate why certain personas answer specific questions correctly while others do not.
Study how output vector circuits in attention heads use earlier-layer representations to shape final predictions.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable versatility in adopting diverse personas. In this study, we examine how assigning a persona influences a model's reasoning on an objective task. Using activation patching, we take a first step toward understanding how key components of the model encode persona-specific information. Our findings reveal that the early Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) layers attend not only to the syntactic structure of the input but also process its semantic content. These layers transform persona tokens into richer representations, which are then used by the middle Multi-Head Attention (MHA) layers to shape the model's output. Additionally, we identify specific attention heads that disproportionately attend to racial and color-based identities.

papers.title: VISIT: Visualizing and Interpreting the Semantic Information Flow of Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we interpret and visualize the semantic information flow inside transformer language models, particularly focusing on attention heads and memory values?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a tool for visualizing the semantic information flow in transformer language models as an interactive flow graph, and provides new insights into layer norms as semantic filters and the existence of regularization neurons.
papers.conclusion: The work introduces a tool to visualize the semantic information flow in transformers using the logit lens, demonstrates its utility by revealing insights about layer norms and regularization neurons, and validates the approach by supporting other analyses.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads' semantics can be projected via the OV circuit, and only the heads with the largest norms dominate the block's output.
Memory values with the highest attention scores capture the semantics of their corresponding attention head.
Layer normalization layers act as semantic filters, demoting function words and promoting content words in the residual stream.
Regularization neurons exist that are consistently highly activated, have high entropy, and may serve as a constant bias or regularization term.
The flow-graph visualization tool can qualitatively replicate mechanistic analyses, such as indirect object identification, and reveal internal information flow patterns.
papers.limitation:
Limited to English language models, particularly GPT models with multi-head attention, and insights might not generalize to other languages or datasets.
Projection methods and the intersection score Ik have limitations in capturing semantic connections between different tokens with the same meaning.
Pruning based on the assumption that the most activated neurons determine the final prediction might be misleading as less activated neurons could also be relevant.
The methods are not causal and do not employ interventions, so further investigation is needed to fully understand the mechanisms.
future_direction: Apply causal interventions to verify the findings.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in interpretability suggest we can project weights and hidden states of transformer-based language models (LMs) to their vocabulary, a transformation that makes them more human interpretable. In this paper, we investigate LM attention heads and memory values, the vectors the models dynamically create and recall while processing a given input. By analyzing the tokens they represent through this projection, we identify patterns in the information flow inside the attention mechanism. Based on our discoveries, we create a tool to visualize a forward pass of Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPTs) as an interactive flow graph, with nodes representing neurons or hidden states and edges representing the interactions between them. Our visualization simplifies huge amounts of data into easy-to-read plots that can reflect the models' internal processing, uncovering the contribution of each component to the models' final prediction. Our visualization also unveils new insights about the role of layer norms as semantic filters that influence the models' output, and about neurons that are always activated during forward passes and act as regularization vectors.

papers.title: Language Models Implement Simple Word2Vec-style Vector Arithmetic
papers.research_question: How do language models solve relational tasks in in-context learning? Do they use a simple vector arithmetic mechanism similar to Word2Vec?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language models implement a simple vector arithmetic mechanism via FFN updates to solve relational tasks in-context, and this mechanism is specific to tasks requiring retrieval from pretraining memory.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that LMs sometimes use simple vector arithmetic mechanisms for relational tasks, offering optimism for interpretability and potential for intervention.
papers.key_findings:
LMs exhibit argument-function processing: they first represent the argument in the residual stream and then apply a function via an FFN update.
The function application is implemented by mid-to-late layer FFNs and is modular (can be transferred to new contexts).
This mechanism is specific to abstractive tasks (requiring retrieval from pretraining memory) and not used in extractive tasks.
The mechanism is similar to Word2Vec-style vector arithmetic and works only for one-to-one relations.
The processing signature becomes sharper with larger models.
papers.limitation:
The intervention is not perfect; errors occur for less frequent associations and due to tokenization.
The mechanism only applies to one-to-one relations, similar to static embeddings.
The intervention procedure may not generalize perfectly across models (e.g., weaker effects on GPT-J).
future_direction: Generalize the findings to model-agnostic phenomena.
Understand how and when different mechanisms for factual recall interact.
Use processing signatures for runtime evaluation and intervention to prevent unwanted behavior.
papers.abstract: Jack Merullo, Carsten Eickhoff, Ellie Pavlick. Proceedings of the 2024 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

papers.title: N-Gram Learning and Pretraining Dynamics in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How do transformer language models acquire capabilities during pretraining, and what is the relationship between n-gram probabilities and this learning process?
papers.core_contribution: The dissertation demonstrates a close relationship between n-gram probabilities and language model learning during pretraining, showing that language model learning is highly dependent on surface-level statistics and identifies bigram subnetworks as a minimal circuit for next token prediction.
papers.conclusion: The results demonstrate a close relationship between n-gram probabilities and language model learning, suggesting that traditional distributional statistics still play a role in complex transformer models. Bigram subnetworks comprise a minimal subset of parameters necessary and sufficient for basic next token predictions.
papers.key_findings:
Language models learn words differently from human children; word frequencies (unigram probabilities) account for the vast majority of variance in words' ages of acquisition in language models, but not in children.
Language model learning can be characterized as early n-gram learning for increasing n, followed by gradual refinement of low-probability n-gram predictions based on longer contexts and more nuanced capabilities.
Subnetworks that make bigram predictions exist in fully trained language models and are critical for model performance, even when they consist of less than 0.2% of model parameters.
Bigram subnetworks are concentrated in the first Transformer MLP layer and overlap significantly with subnetworks trained to optimally prune a given model.
Bigram subnetworks recreate a pattern from the full models where the first layer induces a sharp change that aligns activations with next token predictions rather than current token representations.
papers.limitation:
Surprisal is an imperfect proxy for language model learning; a model might achieve the same surprisal at different points using different internal prediction strategies.
The work only considers language models with 124M parameters trained on 5.1B tokens, and learning curves may differ across model sizes.
future_direction: Further research is necessary to determine the effects of model size on learning speed, variability, and forgetting.
Characterize the examples (e.g., based on types of reasoning, world knowledge, or commonsense) that fluctuate at different points during pre-training across model sizes.
Bigram subnetworks can lay a foundation for studying more complex language model circuits by building up from a minimal circuit.
papers.abstract: Transformer language models have received unprecedented attention in recent years due to impressive performance on natural language tasks, but how they acquire these capabilities is largely unknown. During pretraining, language models are trained to predict next tokens (e.g. words) in text, and the field of pretraining dynamics aims to demonstrate how this learning objective leads to consistent learning patterns and mechanisms. The primary contributions of this dissertation are to demonstrate relationships between n-gram probabilities (next token predictions based only on the previous n-1 tokens) and language model learning during pretraining. I first show that language models learn words differently from human children; word frequencies (unigram probabilities) account for the vast majority of variance in words’ ages of acquisition in language models, but not in children. I then characterize language model learning as early n-gram learning for increasing n, then gradual refinement of low probability n-gram predictions based on longer contexts and more nuanced capabilities. Mechanistically, subnetworks that make bigram predictions exist in the models long after the full models have moved on from simple bigram predictions. These bigram subnetworks are critical to language modeling performance even in fully trained models, and they recreate several key properties of a language model’s activation space across layers. Together, these results demonstrate a close relationship between n-gram probabilities and language model learning, suggesting that traditional distributional statistics still play some role in these more complex models.

papers.title: Restoring Pruned Large Language Models via Lost Component Compensation
papers.research_question: How can we effectively restore the performance of pruned large language models by compensating for the information lost during pruning?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes RestoreLCC, a plug-and-play method that contrastively probes critical attention heads and compensates for pruning-induced lost components via activation editing and injection, effectively restoring pruned model performance while preserving sparsity and inference efficiency.
papers.conclusion: RestoreLCC effectively restores pruned LLMs by compensating for lost components, achieving superior performance recovery compared to existing methods without compromising sparsity or inference efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Reintroducing lost components to selected pruned attention heads can significantly restore model performance.
Different attention heads vary in importance and exhibit distinct recovery behaviors.
Discriminative information may reside in minor components rather than in the principal ones.
RestoreLCC consistently outperforms existing restoration baselines across various pruning schemes and model sizes.
RestoreLCC maintains the sparsity and inference speed of the pruned model while recovering performance.
papers.abstract: Pruning is a widely used technique to reduce the size and inference cost of large language models (LLMs), but it often causes performance degradation. To mitigate this, existing restoration methods typically employ parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), such as LoRA, to recover the pruned model's performance. However, most PEFT methods are designed for dense models and overlook the distinct properties of pruned models, often resulting in suboptimal recovery. In this work, we propose a targeted restoration strategy for pruned models that restores performance while preserving their low cost and high efficiency. We observe that pruning-induced information loss is reflected in attention activations, and selectively reintroducing components of this information can significantly recover model performance. Based on this insight, we introduce RestoreLCC (Restoring Pruned LLMs via Lost Component Compensation), a plug-and-play method that contrastively probes critical attention heads via activation editing, extracts lost components from activation differences, and finally injects them back into the corresponding pruned heads for compensation and recovery. RestoreLCC is compatible with structured, semi-structured, and unstructured pruning schemes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RestoreLCC consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both general and task-specific performance recovery, without compromising the sparsity or inference efficiency of pruned models.

papers.title: Attribution Patching Outperforms Automated Circuit Discovery
papers.research_question: Can a simple method based on attribution patching outperform existing automated circuit discovery techniques in identifying important subnetworks (circuits) within neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Edge Attribution Patching (EAP), a method that uses a linear approximation of activation patching via gradients, outperforms existing automated circuit discovery methods (like ACDC) in recovering known circuits while being significantly more computationally efficient.
papers.conclusion: Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) outperforms ACDC in identifying circuits while being substantially faster, though running ACDC on the subnetwork found by EAP can further improve results.
papers.key_findings:
Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) achieves higher AUC for circuit recovery than ACDC on the IOI and Greater-Than tasks.
EAP is computationally efficient, requiring only two forward passes and one backward pass, unlike ACDC which scales exponentially with the number of nodes.
The linear approximation used in attribution patching can be inaccurate (e.g., concave curves) and may overestimate the effect of ablating an edge.
Running ACDC on the subgraph pruned by EAP can improve circuit identification performance over using EAP alone.
Attribution scores for edges in known circuits (e.g., name movers in IOI) align with their intuitive function, validating the method's outputs.
papers.limitation:
The metrics used for interpretability (like recovery of human-found circuits) do not precisely capture meaningful human understanding.
Human-found circuits are imperfect, which adds noise to the evaluation metric.
The linear approximation in attribution patching can be inaccurate, particularly for edges involving model embeddings, leading to overestimation of edge importance.
future_direction: Future circuit discovery experiments should run EAP first and then apply ACDC on the pruned subgraph.
papers.abstract: Automated interpretability research has recently attracted attention as a potential research direction that could scale explanations of neural network behavior to large models. Existing automated circuit discovery work applies activation patching to identify subnetworks responsible for solving specific tasks (circuits). In this work, we show that a simple method based on attribution patching outperforms all existing methods while requiring just two forward passes and a backward pass. We apply a linear approximation to activation patching to estimate the importance of each edge in the computational subgraph. Using this approximation, we prune the least important edges of the network. We survey the performance and limitations of this method, finding that averaged over all tasks our method has greater AUC from circuit recovery than other methods.

papers.title: Diversity of Transformer Layers: One Aspect of Parameter Scaling Laws
papers.research_question: How do the internal layer dynamics (specifically the diversity of layer outputs) in Transformers relate to parameter scaling laws?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that diversity of predictions from each module in the Transformer residual stream is crucial for performance, and that adding layers improves performance only when layers are diverse, with diminishing returns that align with parameter scaling laws.
papers.conclusion: The diversity of predictions from each module on the residual stream is important for improving Transformer performance, and the effectiveness of adding layers diminishes as the number of layers increases, consistent with parameter scaling laws.
papers.key_findings:
Performance improves when individual layers make predictions close to the correct answer and remain mutually diverse.
Diversity becomes especially critical when individual layers' outputs are far from the ground truth.
Adding layers enhances performance only when those layers behave differently (are diverse).
The performance gains from increasing layers exhibit submodularity: marginal improvements diminish as additional layers increase, mirroring the logarithmic convergence predicted by parameter scaling laws.
Experiments on multiple semantic-understanding tasks with various LLMs empirically confirm these theoretical properties.
papers.limitation: The decomposition based on mean squared error (MSE) is specific to logits, and there may be a gap when targeting tasks that use softmax to obtain probability, such as uncertainty estimation, confidence calibration, and beam decoding. Furthermore, using information-theoretic diversity for actual tasks requires calculating the probability density of the representation on the residual stream, which is difficult without approximation or assumptions.
papers.abstract: Transformers deliver outstanding performance across a wide range of tasks and are now a dominant backbone architecture for large language models (LLMs). Their task-solving performance is improved by increasing parameter size, as shown in the recent studies on parameter scaling laws. Although recent mechanistic-interpretability studies have deepened our understanding of the internal behavior of Transformers by analyzing their residual stream, the relationship between these internal mechanisms and the parameter scaling laws remains unclear. To bridge this gap, we focus on layers and their size, which mainly decide the parameter size of Transformers. For this purpose, we first theoretically investigate the layers within the residual stream through a bias-diversity decomposition. The decomposition separates (i) bias, the error of each layer's output from the ground truth, and (ii) diversity, which indicates how much the outputs of each layer differ from each other. Analyzing Transformers under this theory reveals that performance improves when individual layers make predictions close to the correct answer and remain mutually diverse. We show that diversity becomes especially critical when individual layers' outputs are far from the ground truth. Finally, we introduce an information-theoretic diversity and show our main findings that adding layers enhances performance only when those layers behave differently, i.e., are diverse. We also reveal the performance gains from increasing the number of layers exhibit submodularity: marginal improvements diminish as additional layers increase, mirroring the logarithmic convergence predicted by the parameter scaling laws. Experiments on multiple semantic-understanding tasks with various LLMs empirically confirm the theoretical properties derived in this study.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: How Large Language Models are Designed to Hallucinate
papers.research_question: What is the structural cause of hallucination in large language models, and how does it relate to existential grounding?
papers.core_contribution: Hallucination in LLMs is a structural outcome of the transformer architecture, arising from its flat semantic space that generates coherence without existential grounding such as temporality, mood, and care.
papers.conclusion: Hallucination is the defining limitation of transformer-based LLMs, and future systems must incorporate existential constraints to achieve grounded intelligence.
papers.key_findings:
Distinguishes ontological hallucination (violations of existential structures) from residual reasoning hallucination (mimicking inference without grounding).
Hallucination is persistent and ubiquitous due to the transformer's design as a coherence engine without truth constraints.
Case studies illustrate hallucination failures across existential categories like temporality, mood, and affordances.
Experiment shows extended prompts induce simulated self-preservation language in LLMs, demonstrating coherence pressure.
Scaffolding techniques like retrieval-augmentation mask but do not resolve the structural source of hallucination.
papers.limitation:
The study is illustrative and not exhaustive, with a small sample of models and controlled prompts.
Results may be influenced by scaffolding strategies like fine-tuning and safety filters in frontier models.
More systematic benchmarks are needed to fully evaluate hallucination across existential categories.
future_direction: Design systematic evaluations aligned with existential categories such as temporality, mood, and affordances.
Explore architectural prototypes that embed structural constraints like temporal ordering or affordance maps.
Investigate training objectives that reward withholding or deferring when disclosure is absent.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve remarkable fluency across linguistic and reasoning tasks but remain systematically prone to hallucination. Prevailing accounts attribute hallucinations to data gaps, limited context, or optimization errors. We argue instead that hallucination is a structural outcome of the transformer architecture. As coherence engines, transformers are compelled to produce fluent continuations, with self-attention simulating the relational structure of meaning but lacking the existential grounding of temporality, mood, and care that stabilizes human understanding. On this basis, we distinguish ontological hallucination, arising when continuations require disclosure of beings in world, and residual reasoning hallucination, where models mimic inference by recycling traces of human reasoning in text. We illustrate these patterns through case studies aligned with Heideggerian categories and an experiment across twelve LLMs showing how simulated "self-preservation" emerges under extended prompts. Our contribution is threefold: (1) a comparative account showing why existing explanations are insufficient; (2) a predictive taxonomy of hallucination linked to existential structures with proposed benchmarks; and (3) design directions toward "truth-constrained" architectures capable of withholding or deferring when disclosure is absent. We conclude that hallucination is not an incidental defect but a defining limit of transformer-based models, an outcome scaffolding can mask but never resolve.

papers.title: Finding Transformer Circuits with Edge Pruning
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently and accurately discover sparse computational subgraphs (circuits) in transformers that capture specific model behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Edge Pruning, an efficient and scalable gradient-based pruning method for automated circuit discovery that finds sparser and more faithful circuits than prior methods.
papers.conclusion: Edge Pruning is a practical and scalable tool for interpretability that can shed light on behaviors emerging in large models.
papers.key_findings:
Edge Pruning finds circuits in GPT-2 that use less than half the edges of prior methods while being equally faithful on standard tasks.
The method scales effectively to 100K examples and to CodeLlama-13B, a model over 100x larger than GPT-2.
It perfectly recovers ground-truth circuits in Tracr-compiled models.
A case study on CodeLlama-13B reveals substantial overlap between circuits for instruction-prompted and in-context learning settings, suggesting shared mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
The method's reliance on providing corrupted examples for interchange ablation.
Potential challenges in converging to very high sparsity regimes.
future_direction: Improving the efficiency and scalability of the method further.
Applying Edge Pruning to more complex tasks and model behaviors.
Exploring the method's applicability to other model architectures.
papers.abstract: The path to interpreting a language model often proceeds via analysis of circuits -- sparse computational subgraphs of the model that capture specific aspects of its behavior. Recent work has automated the task of discovering circuits. Yet, these methods have practical limitations, as they rely either on inefficient search algorithms or inaccurate approximations. In this paper, we frame automated circuit discovery as an optimization problem and propose *Edge Pruning* as an effective and scalable solution. Edge Pruning leverages gradient-based pruning techniques, but instead of removing neurons or components, it prunes the \emph{edges} between components. Our method finds circuits in GPT-2 that use less than half the number of edges compared to circuits found by previous methods while being equally faithful to the full model predictions on standard circuit-finding tasks. Edge Pruning is efficient even with as many as 100K examples, outperforming previous methods in speed and producing substantially better circuits. It also perfectly recovers the ground-truth circuits in two models compiled with Tracr. Thanks to its efficiency, we scale Edge Pruning to CodeLlama-13B, a model over 100x the scale that prior methods operate on. We use this setting for a case study comparing the mechanisms behind instruction prompting and in-context learning. We find two circuits with more than 99.96% sparsity that match the performance of the full model and reveal that the mechanisms in the two settings overlap substantially. Our case study shows that Edge Pruning is a practical and scalable tool for interpretability and sheds light on behaviors that only emerge in large models.

papers.title: Cyclic Ablation: Testing Concept Localization against Functional Regeneration in AI
papers.research_question: Whether undesirable behaviors like deception are localized functions that can be removed, or if they are deeply intertwined with a model's core cognitive abilities.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces cyclic ablation to test concept localization, demonstrating that deception in DistilGPT-2 is distributed and resilient, with ablation leading to functional regeneration and gradual linguistic performance decay.
papers.conclusion: Highlights limitations of ablation for removing undesirable behavior, suggesting complex concepts are resilient states deeply intertwined with core capabilities, pointing to the need for more subtle steering methods.
papers.key_findings:
Deception is highly resilient and recovers after ablation via adversarial training, a process termed functional regeneration.
Ablation causes a gradual increase in perplexity, indicating degradation of linguistic competence.
SAE features are fragile under fine-tuning and require dynamic identification to remain valid.
The representation for deception is redundant and distributed, with the model finding alternative neural pathways to restore the function.
Attempts to remove deception damage overall model performance, suggesting features are polysemantic and involved in legitimate computations.
papers.limitation:
Conducted on a relatively small model.
Definition of deception was highly specialized, while the dataset might be a potential source of bias.
Lack of control runs with ablation of random features.
future_direction: Investigating larger models with greater redundancy and different regeneration mechanisms.
Investigating more subtle forms of deception.
Adding control runs with ablation of random features to strengthen evidence.
papers.abstract: Safety and controllability are critical for large language models. A central question is whether undesirable behaviors like deception are localized functions that can be removed, or if they are deeply intertwined with a model's core cognitive abilities. We introduce "cyclic ablation," an iterative method to test this. By combining sparse autoencoders, targeted ablation, and adversarial training on DistilGPT-2, we attempted to eliminate the concept of deception. We found that, contrary to the localization hypothesis, deception was highly resilient. The model consistently recovered its deceptive behavior after each ablation cycle via adversarial training, a process we term functional regeneration. Crucially, every attempt at this "neurosurgery" caused a gradual but measurable decay in general linguistic performance, reflected by a consistent rise in perplexity. These findings are consistent with the view that complex concepts are distributed and entangled, underscoring the limitations of direct model editing through mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Causal interventions expose implicit situation models for commonsense language understanding
papers.research_question: How do transformer models construct implicit situation models to guide pronoun resolution in commonsense language understanding?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a circuit of attention heads responsible for propagating contextual information in transformer models for pronoun resolution, using causal interventions and controlled datasets.
papers.conclusion: The study provides preliminary evidence for distinct neural pathways underlying implicit situation models in transformer models, highlighting the value of causal interventions for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
A small circuit of attention heads propagates information from context words to guide pronoun resolution.
Syntax-based pronoun resolution uses more localized pathways compared to context-based resolution involving situation models.
Larger models like ALBERT-xxlarge show better performance and more distinct circuits for situation models.
papers.limitation: Single-site interchange interventions may over-count synergies and under-count redundancies in circuits.
future_direction: Explore settings requiring richer interpretations beyond pronoun resolution.
Use chain-of-thought prompting to expose situation models more explicitly in auto-regressive models.
papers.abstract: Accounts of human language processing have long appealed to implicit ``situation models'' that enrich comprehension with relevant but unstated world knowledge. Here, we apply causal intervention techniques to recent transformer models to analyze performance on the Winograd Schema Challenge (WSC), where a single context cue shifts interpretation of an ambiguous pronoun. We identify a relatively small circuit of attention heads that are responsible for propagating information from the context word that guides which of the candidate noun phrases the pronoun ultimately attends to. We then compare how this circuit behaves in a closely matched ``syntactic'' control where the situation model is not strictly necessary. These analyses suggest distinct pathways through which implicit situation models are constructed to guide pronoun resolution.

papers.title: Journey to the Center of the Knowledge Neurons: Discoveries of Language-Independent Knowledge Neurons and Degenerate Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge stored in multilingual pre-trained language models, and what are the properties of the neurons that store such knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Architecture-adapted Multilingual Integrated Gradients (AMIG) method for precise knowledge neuron localization in multilingual PLMs, and discovers two new types of neurons: language-independent knowledge neurons and degenerate knowledge neurons.
papers.conclusion: The AMIG method effectively localizes knowledge neurons in multilingual PLMs, and the discoveries of language-independent and degenerate knowledge neurons shed light on the mechanisms of factual knowledge storage.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed AMIG method localizes knowledge neurons more precisely than baseline methods, especially for Chinese datasets.
Knowledge neurons in m-BERT are primarily in the final layers, while in m-GPT they are distributed across early, middle, and final layers.
Language-independent knowledge neurons exist, are concentrated in the final layers, and facilitate cross-lingual knowledge editing.
Degenerate knowledge neurons exist, exhibit functional overlap, and can be used to help PLMs detect wrong facts in a fact-checking task.
The existence of degenerate knowledge neurons is not dependent on multilingualism, as they are also found in monolingual models (BERT and GPT-2).
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models (PLMs) contain vast amounts of factual knowledge, but how the knowledge is stored in the parameters remains unclear. This paper delves into the complex task of understanding how factual knowledge is stored in multilingual PLMs, and introduces the Architecture-adapted Multilingual Integrated Gradients method, which successfully localizes knowledge neurons more precisely compared to current methods, and is more universal across various architectures and languages. Moreover, we conduct an in-depth exploration on knowledge neurons, leading to the following two important discoveries: (1) The discovery of Language-Independent Knowledge Neurons, which store factual knowledge in a form that transcends language. We design cross-lingual knowledge editing experiments, demonstrating that the PLMs can accomplish this task based on language-independent neurons; (2) The discovery of Degenerate Knowledge Neurons, a novel type of neuron showing that different knowledge neurons can store the same fact. Its property of functional overlap endows the PLMs with a robust mastery of factual knowledge. We design fact-checking experiments, proving that the degenerate knowledge neurons can help the PLMs to detect wrong facts. Experiments corroborate these findings, shedding light on the mechanisms of factual knowledge storage in multilingual PLMs, and contribute valuable insights to the field. The code is available at https://github.com/heng840/AMIG.

papers.title: minicons: Enabling Flexible Behavioral and Representational Analyses of Transformer Language Models
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces minicons, an open-source library that provides a standard API for behavioral and representational analyses of transformer language models, facilitating efficient extraction of word/sentence probabilities and contextualized embeddings.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents minicons, a utility tool for analyzing transformer language models, and demonstrates its use in two case studies, showing its potential for facilitating behavioral and representational analyses.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's knowledge of linguistic acceptability emerges at different rates for different phenomena, with some phenomena showing signs of forgetting during training.
On zero-shot abductive reasoning, most models perform near chance, with ALBERT-xxlarge-v2 achieving the best accuracy (0.61) despite being smaller than other models.
Performance on abductive reasoning scales linearly with the logarithm of the number of parameters (R²=0.48), suggesting that scaling alone is unlikely to reach state-of-the-art performance.
future_direction: Integrate newer utility functions into the library and develop detailed tutorials for users.
papers.abstract: We present minicons, an open source library that provides a standard API for researchers interested in conducting behavioral and representational analyses of transformer-based language models (LMs). Specifically, minicons enables researchers to apply analysis methods at two levels: (1) at the prediction level -- by providing functions to efficiently extract word/sentence level probabilities; and (2) at the representational level -- by also facilitating efficient extraction of word/phrase level vectors from one or more layers. In this paper, we describe the library and apply it to two motivating case studies: One focusing on the learning dynamics of the BERT architecture on relative grammatical judgments, and the other on benchmarking 23 different LMs on zero-shot abductive reasoning. minicons is available at https://github.com/kanishkamisra/minicons

papers.title: Cracking Factual Knowledge: A Comprehensive Analysis of Degenerate Knowledge Neurons in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How are degenerate knowledge neurons (DKNs) defined and acquired, and what is their relationship to the robustness, evolvability, and complexity of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a comprehensive definition of degenerate knowledge neurons (DKNs) from structural and functional perspectives and introduces the Neurological Topology Clustering method for accurate DKN acquisition, demonstrating that DKNs are linked to the robustness, evolvability, and complexity of large language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a comprehensive definition of DKNs and introduces the neurological topology clustering method for precise DKN acquisition, and through extensive experiments demonstrates the critical role of DKNs in the robustness, evolvability, and complexity of PLMs.
papers.key_findings:
DKNs identified by the Neurological Topology Clustering method exhibit strong degeneracy, meaning suppressing a subset of Base Degenerate Components (BDCs) does not significantly affect prediction probability, while suppressing all BDCs does.
DKNs help PLMs cope with input interference, indicating their contribution to model robustness.
DKNs have strong fact-checking ability, outperforming knowledge neurons and direct PLM-based fact-checking.
PLMs utilize DKNs to learn new knowledge, as parameter changes during fine-tuning highly overlap with DKNs.
Efficient fine-tuning by freezing all MLP neurons except DKNs enables PLMs to learn new knowledge while preserving old knowledge, highlighting DKNs' role in evolvability.
papers.limitation:
Limited to GPT-2 and LLaMA2-7b models; validation on larger models is needed.
Confined to factual knowledge; applicability to other knowledge types is unknown.
Generalizability across different languages and cultural contexts is an open question due to the use of English datasets.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) store extensive factual knowledge, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Previous research suggests that factual knowledge is stored within multi-layer perceptron weights, and some storage units exhibit degeneracy, referred to as Degenerate Knowledge Neurons (DKNs). Despite the novelty and unique properties of this concept, it has not been rigorously defined or systematically studied. We first consider the connection weight patterns of MLP neurons and define DKNs from both structural and functional aspects. Based on this, we introduce the Neurological Topology Clustering method, which allows the formation of DKNs in any numbers and structures, leading to a more accurate DKN acquisition. Furthermore, inspired by cognitive science, we explore the relationship between DKNs and the robustness, evolvability, and complexity of LLMs. Our execution of 34 experiments under 6 settings demonstrates the connection between DKNs and these three properties. The code will be available soon.

papers.title: The Bayesian Geometry of Transformer Attention
papers.research_question: Can transformers perform exact Bayesian inference, or do they merely approximate it through pattern matching?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides the first empirical proof that neural sequence models can realize exact Bayesian posteriors, introduces Bayesian wind tunnels as a tool for probing algorithmic reasoning in verifiable settings, and establishes a taxonomy of inference primitives that explains which architectures succeed on which tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that Bayesian inference is not monolithic and decomposes into primitives; transformers succeed by realizing all primitives, while other architectures realize subsets, explaining their performance differences.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers achieve exact Bayesian posteriors with sub-bit calibration error across multiple inference tasks.
Mamba realizes belief accumulation and transport but struggles with random-access binding, excelling on HMM filtering but not on associative recall.
LSTMs realize only accumulation of static sufficient statistics and fail when inference requires transport or binding.
MLPs fail uniformly on all Bayesian inference tasks.
Geometric diagnostics reveal orthogonal key bases, low-dimensional value manifolds parameterized by entropy, and in Mamba, discrete clusters corresponding to HMM hidden states.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are small-scale with controlled Bayesian wind tunnels, modest vocabulary sizes, and small models, abstracting away from natural-language complexity.
Tasks capture only a narrow slice of inference problems (e.g., discrete elimination and recursive state tracking), not richer latent-variable structures.
Hypothesis spaces have modest representational dimensionality, not testing high-dimensional latent variables.
Connection to large pretrained models remains an open question; it's unclear if similar Bayesian manifolds arise in natural language settings.
Architectural generality is limited to standard transformers; alternative architectures may form comparable manifolds but were not fully explored.
future_direction: Extend wind tunnels to richer latent-variable structures like Kalman filtering or hierarchical Bayesian models.
Test whether geometric mechanisms scale smoothly with higher-dimensional hypothesis spaces.
Apply geometric diagnostics to frontier LLMs to search for Bayesian signatures in pretrained models.
Evaluate alternative architectures (e.g., state-space models, hybrid systems) using wind-tunnel benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Transformers often appear to perform Bayesian reasoning in context, but verifying this rigorously has been impossible: natural data lack analytic posteriors, and large models conflate reasoning with memorization. We address this by constructing \emph{Bayesian wind tunnels} -- controlled environments where the true posterior is known in closed form and memorization is provably impossible. In these settings, small transformers reproduce Bayesian posteriors with $10^{-3}$-$10^{-4}$ bit accuracy, while capacity-matched MLPs fail by orders of magnitude, establishing a clear architectural separation. Across two tasks -- bijection elimination and Hidden Markov Model (HMM) state tracking -- we find that transformers implement Bayesian inference through a consistent geometric mechanism: residual streams serve as the belief substrate, feed-forward networks perform the posterior update, and attention provides content-addressable routing. Geometric diagnostics reveal orthogonal key bases, progressive query-key alignment, and a low-dimensional value manifold parameterized by posterior entropy. During training this manifold unfurls while attention patterns remain stable, a \emph{frame-precision dissociation} predicted by recent gradient analyses. Taken together, these results demonstrate that hierarchical attention realizes Bayesian inference by geometric design, explaining both the necessity of attention and the failure of flat architectures. Bayesian wind tunnels provide a foundation for mechanistically connecting small, verifiable systems to reasoning phenomena observed in large language models.

papers.title: How Language Models Conflate Logical Validity with Plausibility: A Representational Analysis of Content Effects
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode the concepts of validity and plausibility, and why do they conflate them, leading to content effects in reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that validity and plausibility are linearly represented and aligned in LLMs, causing content effects, and that steering vectors can disentangle these concepts to reduce bias and improve reasoning accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The representational entanglement of validity and plausibility in LLMs leads to content effects, and representational interventions offer a way to mitigate these biases for more logical reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit content effects where plausibility influences validity judgments, especially in zero-shot settings.
Validity and plausibility are linearly encoded as single directions in the model's activation space, and these vectors are highly similar.
The degree of alignment between validity and plausibility vectors predicts the magnitude of behavioral content effects across models.
Plausibility vectors can causally bias validity judgments, and vice versa, demonstrating cross-concept influence.
Debiasing steering vectors that disentangle validity from plausibility can reduce content effects and improve reasoning accuracy.
papers.abstract: Both humans and large language models (LLMs) exhibit content effects: biases in which the plausibility of the semantic content of a reasoning problem influences judgments regarding its logical validity. While this phenomenon in humans is best explained by the dual-process theory of reasoning, the mechanisms behind content effects in LLMs remain unclear. In this work, we address this issue by investigating how LLMs encode the concepts of validity and plausibility within their internal representations. We show that both concepts are linearly represented and strongly aligned in representational geometry, leading models to conflate plausibility with validity. Using steering vectors, we demonstrate that plausibility vectors can causally bias validity judgements, and vice versa, and that the degree of alignment between these two concepts predicts the magnitude of behavioral content effects across models. Finally, we construct debiasing vectors that disentangle these concepts, reducing content effects and improving reasoning accuracy. Our findings advance understanding of how abstract logical concepts are represented in LLMs and highlight representational interventions as a path toward more logical systems.

papers.title: Seeking Neural Nuggets: Knowledge Transfer in Large Language Models from a Parametric Perspective
papers.research_question: Whether implicit knowledge stored in the parameters of a larger language model (teacher) can be transferred to a smaller model (student) through a parametric perspective.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a parametric knowledge transfer paradigm that extracts task-specific parameters from a teacher model using sensitivity-based techniques and injects them into a student model via LoRA, demonstrating the transferability of implicit knowledge across LLMs of different scales.
papers.conclusion: Parametric knowledge transfer is feasible and effective; the proposed framework successfully transfers knowledge from larger to smaller LLMs, and the analysis highlights key factors that contribute to successful transfer.
papers.key_findings:
Transferring extracted parameters from a teacher to a student model consistently improves the student's performance across reasoning, professional knowledge, instruction-driven, and open-ended conversation benchmarks.
The structural integrity of the extracted parameters (e.g., preserving submatrices) is crucial for effective transfer, outperforming random or single-weight extraction.
Sensitivity-based parameter extraction outperforms random selection, and the origin of parameters (which modules) matters more than the sheer number of parameters transferred.
Scaling up the teacher model generally leads to better student performance, even when there are architectural differences between models.
The number of seed samples used for sensitivity calculation and the initialization strategy for the LoRA module are important factors influencing transfer efficacy.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) inherently encode a wealth of knowledge within their parameters through pre-training on extensive corpora. While prior research has delved into operations on these parameters to manipulate the underlying implicit knowledge (encompassing detection, editing, and merging), there remains an ambiguous understanding regarding their transferability across models with varying scales. In this paper, we seek to empirically investigate knowledge transfer from larger to smaller models through a parametric perspective. To achieve this, we employ sensitivity-based techniques to extract and align knowledge-specific parameters between different LLMs. Moreover, the LoRA module is used as the intermediary mechanism for injecting the extracted knowledge into smaller models. Evaluations across four benchmarks validate the efficacy of our proposed method. Our findings highlight the critical factors contributing to the process of parametric knowledge transfer, underscoring the transferability of model parameters across LLMs of different scales. Project website: https://maszhongming.github.io/ParaKnowTransfer.

papers.title: From Concepts to Components: Concept-Agnostic Attention Module Discovery in Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we map arbitrary, complex concepts to specific attention heads in transformer models in a concept-agnostic way, and how can we intervene on these modules to control model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a concept-agnostic method (SAMD) to map arbitrary concepts to sparse sets of attention heads in transformers, and a simple intervention strategy (SAMI) to diminish or amplify these concepts by scaling the heads' outputs with a single scalar parameter.
papers.conclusion: The proposed pipeline enables concept-agnostic attention head attribution and effective intervention for arbitrary concepts in transformers, offering new insights into the role of attention in concept encoding and control.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge for a wide variety of concepts is sparsely encoded in only 3-10 attention heads across transformer models.
The locations of concept-associated attention modules remain stable before and after LLM post-training, supporting the superficial alignment hypothesis.
The 'French' module is located in later layers, confirming prior work that multilingual LLMs 'think' in English and translate later.
Diminishing the safety module via SAMI increases jailbreaking success on HarmBench by up to +72.7%.
Amplifying the reasoning module improves performance on GSM8K by +1.6%, and suppressing a recognition module in a ViT reduces target label accuracy to 0%.
papers.limitation:
The method does not establish causality for the identified modules, which could be overcomplete or incomplete.
No theoretical sample complexity or stability analysis is provided.
papers.abstract: Transformers have achieved state-of-the-art performance across language and vision tasks. This success drives the imperative to interpret their internal mechanisms with the dual goals of enhancing performance and improving behavioral control. Attribution methods help advance interpretability by assigning model outputs associated with a target concept to specific model components. Current attribution research primarily studies multi-layer perceptron neurons and addresses relatively simple concepts such as factual associations (e.g., Paris is located in France). This focus tends to overlook the impact of the attention mechanism and lacks a unified approach for analyzing more complex concepts. To fill these gaps, we introduce Scalable Attention Module Discovery (SAMD), a concept-agnostic method for mapping arbitrary, complex concepts to specific attention heads of general transformer models. We accomplish this by representing each concept as a vector, calculating its cosine similarity with each attention head, and selecting the TopK-scoring heads to construct the concept-associated attention module. We then propose Scalar Attention Module Intervention (SAMI), a simple strategy to diminish or amplify the effects of a concept by adjusting the attention module using only a single scalar parameter. Empirically, we demonstrate SAMD on concepts of varying complexity, and visualize the locations of their corresponding modules. Our results demonstrate that module locations remain stable before and after LLM post-training, and confirm prior work on the mechanics of LLM multilingualism. Through SAMI, we facilitate jailbreaking on HarmBench (+72.7%) by diminishing "safety" and improve performance on the GSM8K benchmark (+1.6%) by amplifying "reasoning". Lastly, we highlight the domain-agnostic nature of our approach by suppressing the image classification accuracy of vision transformers on ImageNet.

papers.title: Mechanistic Evidence for Faithfulness Decay in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning reflect the model's actual decision-making process, or is it merely post-hoc justification?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NLDD, a metric for step-level faithfulness in chain-of-thought reasoning, and discovers a consistent Reasoning Horizon (k*) at 70–85% of chain length beyond which reasoning tokens have little or negative effect on the final answer.
papers.conclusion: NLDD quantifies the causal influence of reasoning chains on model predictions, revealing that high accuracy can mask a lack of causal dependence on CoT, and identifies a reasoning horizon beyond which steps contribute minimally or negatively.
papers.key_findings:
Different architectures exhibit distinct faithfulness patterns (faithful vs. anti-faithful regimes).
The Mapping Gap demonstrates models can encode task-relevant structure in internal representations without utilizing it for prediction.
The reasoning horizon (k*) is a consistent transition point at 70-85% of chain length where causal influence decays.
NLDD reveals failure modes that accuracy-based evaluation misses, such as anti-faithful behavior.
For anti-faithful models, extended reasoning beyond the horizon can be harmful, acting as a causal distractor.
papers.limitation:
Truncates chains rather than replacing corrupted steps, which conflates weak reliance on a step with sufficiency of prior steps.
Logit normalization assumes architectural differences affect margins and variance proportionally, which is empirically supported but not guaranteed.
TAS and RSA analysis uses a single middle layer; layer-wise variation is small but comprehensive analysis may reveal depth-dependent effects.
Evaluation is limited to three tasks (100 samples each), two of which are synthetic, and to decoder-only models.
Uses greedy decoding with fixed prompts; stochastic decoding may shift horizon locations.
Step-based analysis assumes explicit chain structure; free-form CoT would require different segmentation.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) explanations are widely used to interpret how language models solve complex problems, yet it remains unclear whether these step-by-step explanations reflect how the model actually reaches its answer, or merely post-hoc justifications. We propose Normalized Logit Difference Decay (NLDD), a metric that measures whether individual reasoning steps are faithful to the model's decision-making process. Our approach corrupts individual reasoning steps from the explanation and measures how much the model's confidence in its answer drops, to determine if a step is truly important. By standardizing these measurements, NLDD enables rigorous cross-model comparison across different architectures. Testing three model families across syntactic, logical, and arithmetic tasks, we discover a consistent Reasoning Horizon (k*) at 70--85% of chain length, beyond which reasoning tokens have little or negative effect on the final answer. We also find that models can encode correct internal representations while completely failing the task. These results show that accuracy alone does not reveal whether a model actually reasons through its chain. NLDD offers a way to measure when CoT matters.

papers.title: ELICIT: LLM Augmentation via External In-Context Capability
papers.research_question: Can we elicit and harness the potential of LLMs’ inherent capabilities when adapting to new tasks, as demonstrated by ICL, while simultaneously maintaining efficiency and flexibility?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ELICIT, a framework that stores and reuses task vectors (derived from in-context learning demonstrations) to elicit model capabilities without extra training or inference tokens.
papers.conclusion: ELICIT serves as a plug-and-play performance booster to enable adaptive elicitation of model capabilities by externally storing and reusing task vectors.
papers.key_findings:
ELICIT improves zero-shot performance by an average of 11.4% across 20 tasks and 4 models without increasing token usage.
ELICIT can selectively activate capabilities (e.g., a math-only library boosts math performance while maintaining others).
ELICIT is complementary to existing methods like BM25 retrieval, further improving performance.
ELICIT generalizes to unseen tasks and different input formats.
The additive intervention strategy (˜hl = hl + 2 × θl) balances task performance and language modeling capability.
future_direction: Comprehensive adaptation of ELICIT for instruction-tuned models.
Improving the quality of task vectors through better demonstration selection methods.
Exploring the mechanisms and benefits of multi-layer interventions.
papers.abstract: Enhancing the adaptive capabilities of large language models is a critical pursuit in both research and application. Traditional fine-tuning methods require substantial data and computational resources, especially for enhancing specific capabilities, while in-context learning is limited by the need for appropriate demonstrations and efficient token usage. Inspired by the expression of in-context learned capabilities through task vectors and the concept of modularization, we propose \alg, a framework consisting of two modules designed to effectively store and reuse task vectors to elicit the diverse capabilities of models without additional training or inference tokens. Our comprehensive experiments and analysis demonstrate that our pipeline is highly transferable across different input formats, tasks, and model architectures. ELICIT serves as a plug-and-play performance booster to enable adaptive elicitation of model capabilities. By externally storing and reusing vectors that represent in-context learned capabilities, \alg not only demonstrates the potential to operate modular capabilities but also significantly enhances the performance, versatility, adaptability, and scalability of large language models. Our code will be publicly available at https://github.com/LINs-lab/ELICIT.

papers.title: From Yes-Men to Truth-Tellers: Addressing Sycophancy in Large Language Models with Pinpoint Tuning
papers.research_question: How can we address sycophancy in Large Language Models by pinpointing and tuning only the components responsible for this behavior, without degrading their general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes supervised pinpoint tuning (SPT), a method that identifies a sparse set of attention heads responsible for sycophancy using path patching and then fine-tunes only those heads, effectively mitigating sycophancy while preserving the model's general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Pinpoint tuning is an effective and efficient method to address sycophancy in LLMs by targeting specific internal components, advancing both the understanding and intervention of model behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Only a small percentage (~4%) of attention heads significantly influence sycophantic behavior, as identified by path patching.
Pinpoint tuning these heads effectively reduces sycophancy, outperforming supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on sycophancy metrics.
Pinpoint tuning preserves general capabilities (e.g., reasoning, math, code) unlike SFT, which often degrades them.
The method generalizes beyond the training data, as shown on additional sycophancy evaluation datasets.
The identified sycophancy-related heads attend more to tokens that challenge the model compared to other heads.
papers.limitation:
Path patching treats each MLP and attention head as individual nodes, but future work could consider neurons or groups of neurons as atomic units for more refined analysis.
The evaluation is based on a specific definition of sycophancy (from Sharma et al. 2023), and it is unclear whether the results generalize to other formats of sycophancy.
The verification of pinpoint tuning is mainly conducted on sycophancy; its effectiveness for other abilities requires further investigation.
future_direction: Treating neurons or groups of neurons as atomic units for analysis instead of heads and MLPs.
Investigating generalization to other formats and definitions of sycophancy.
Integrating pinpoint tuning with other interpretability tools like information flow, representation engineering, and sparse auto-encoders.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) tend to prioritize adherence to user prompts over providing veracious responses, leading to the sycophancy issue. When challenged by users, LLMs tend to admit mistakes and provide inaccurate responses even if they initially provided the correct answer. Recent works propose to employ supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to mitigate the sycophancy issue, while it typically leads to the degeneration of LLMs' general capability. To address the challenge, we propose a novel supervised pinpoint tuning (SPT), where the region-of-interest modules are tuned for a given objective. Specifically, SPT first reveals and verifies a small percentage (<5%) of the basic modules, which significantly affect a particular behavior of LLMs. i.e., sycophancy. Subsequently, SPT merely fine-tunes these identified modules while freezing the rest. To verify the effectiveness of the proposed SPT, we conduct comprehensive experiments, demonstrating that SPT significantly mitigates the sycophancy issue of LLMs (even better than SFT). Moreover, SPT introduces limited or even no side effects on the general capability of LLMs. Our results shed light on how to precisely, effectively, and efficiently explain and improve the targeted ability of LLMs. Code and data are available at https://github.com/yellowtownhz/sycophancy-interpretability.

papers.title: From Directions to Cones: Exploring Multidimensional Representations of Propositional Facts in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does truth in LLMs have a multi-dimensional representation (concept cone) rather than a single linear direction, and can such cones causally mediate truth-related behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that truth in LLMs is represented as a multi-dimensional cone in activation space, and that interventions using these cones can reliably steer model outputs on true/false propositions while preserving unrelated capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Multi-dimensional concept cones can reliably steer LLM behavior on true/false propositions across architectures and sizes, revealing a robust subspace of activation vectors that modulate factuality.
papers.key_findings:
Truth-related directions are localized in middle to later layers, with the final token position being most effective for interventions.
Multi-dimensional concept cones for truth exist and can causally mediate truthful behavior across different model families and sizes.
Increasing cone dimensionality generally improves steering effectiveness, but beyond a point, ASR declines, especially in smaller models.
The discovered truth directions are specific and do not significantly affect general instruction-following capabilities (low KL divergence on Alpaca).
The classic DIM direction aligns only with the first axis of the cone; other axes are orthogonal, indicating additional structure.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on relatively small open-source models (1.5B–7B parameters) and may not generalize to larger frontier models.
The operationalization of truth is narrow, limited to simple unambiguous propositional facts, and does not capture more complex notions of truth.
The method does not guarantee discovery of a maximally informative or interpretable subspace, and individual cone axes lack semantic meaning.
future_direction: Pair cones with automated clustering or sparse autoencoding to assign semantic meaning to basis vectors.
Extend the method to larger, instruction-tuned models.
Extend to multimodal settings.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong conversational abilities but often generate falsehoods. Prior work suggests that the truthfulness of simple propositions can be represented as a single linear direction in a model's internal activations, but this may not fully capture its underlying geometry. In this work, we extend the concept cone framework, recently introduced for modeling refusal, to the domain of truth. We identify multi-dimensional cones that causally mediate truth-related behavior across multiple LLM families. Our results are supported by three lines of evidence: (i) causal interventions reliably flip model responses to factual statements, (ii) learned cones generalize across model architectures, and (iii) cone-based interventions preserve unrelated model behavior. These findings reveal the richer, multidirectional structure governing simple true/false propositions in LLMs and highlight concept cones as a promising tool for probing abstract behaviors.

papers.title: Brittle Minds, Fixable Activations: Understanding Belief Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do internal belief representations emerge in language models? Are they structured or spurious? How robust are they to prompt variations? Can they be strengthened?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that belief representations in language models improve with model size and fine-tuning, are structured yet brittle to prompt variations, and can be strengthened using contrastive activation addition to correct wrong Theory of Mind inferences.
papers.conclusion: Belief representations in language models are structured but brittle, and they can be strengthened via activation editing, offering a path toward more reliable Theory of Mind reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Belief representations emerge in consistent patterns across models, improve with model size, and benefit significantly from fine-tuning, especially in smaller models.
Control tasks and PCA show that belief representations are structured and not spurious.
Representations of others' beliefs are brittle to semantically neutral prompt variations.
Contrastive activation addition (CAA) can strengthen belief representations and improve ToM performance across different tasks.
CAA steering vectors are general and transferable to other ToM tasks, yielding substantial performance gains.
papers.limitation:
The study focused on one dataset (BigToM) and a limited set of model families due to computational constraints.
The approach could be extended to other mental states beyond beliefs.
future_direction: Exploring how different types of fine-tuning influence the emergence of internal belief representations.
Developing robustness benchmarks and new approaches to improve generalization of belief representations.
Directly embedding perspective-taking circuits into model architectures.
papers.abstract: Despite growing interest in Theory of Mind (ToM) tasks for evaluating language models (LMs), little is known about how LMs internally represent mental states of self and others. Understanding these internal mechanisms is critical - not only to move beyond surface-level performance, but also for model alignment and safety, where subtle misattributions of mental states may go undetected in generated outputs. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation of belief representations in LMs by probing models across different scales, training regimens, and prompts - using control tasks to rule out confounds. Our experiments provide evidence that both model size and fine-tuning substantially improve LMs' internal representations of others' beliefs, which are structured - not mere by-products of spurious correlations - yet brittle to prompt variations. Crucially, we show that these representations can be strengthened: targeted edits to model activations can correct wrong ToM inferences.

papers.title: How large language models encode theory-of-mind: a study on sparse parameter patterns
papers.research_question: Which parameters in LLMs are sensitive to Theory-of-Mind capabilities, and how do these parameters influence ToM reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to identify extremely sparse ToM-sensitive parameters in LLMs and shows that these parameters are linked to RoPE positional encoding, affecting attention mechanisms and degrading ToM performance when perturbed.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that ToM capabilities in LLMs are governed by sparse, low-rank parameter patterns linked to positional encoding and attention mechanisms, providing insights into how LLMs perform social reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
An extremely sparse ToM-sensitive parameter pattern exists, whose perturbation significantly affects RoPE-based models' ToM capabilities, while random perturbations do not. This degradation is linked to a reduction in contextual localization and language understanding.
The functionality of the ToM-sensitive parameter pattern relates to the positional encoding module in LLM architectures. Perturbing the pattern in LLMs with RoPE disrupts dominant frequency activations, impairing contextual localization. LLMs without RoPE lack this frequency-dependent activation structure and exhibit different sensitivity patterns.
Perturbing ToM-sensitive parameter patterns affects the attention mechanism, thereby influencing language understanding. It alters the angle between q and k_BOS under positional encoding, destabilizing the attention sink and distorting the attention matrix.
papers.limitation: The study focuses only on false-belief tasks (unexpected contents and transfer) and does not evaluate the full spectrum of ToM abilities.
future_direction: Leveraging ToM-sensitive parameters for targeted model alignment to ensure AI systems align with human ethical norms while mitigating unintended social biases.
Comparing the identified sparse parameter structures to neural representations of ToM in the human brain for comparative cognitive modeling.
Investigating if targeted attacks could degrade LLM reasoning abilities given that ToM capabilities depend on sparse and structured parameter subsets, for robustness and adversarial testing.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the emergence of Theory-of-Mind (ToM) capabilities in large language models (LLMs) from a mechanistic perspective, focusing on the role of extremely sparse parameter patterns. We introduce a novel method to identify ToM-sensitive parameters and reveal that perturbing as little as 0.001% of these parameters significantly degrades ToM performance while also impairing contextual localization and language understanding. To understand this effect, we analyze their interactions with core architectural components of LLMs. Our findings demonstrate that these sensitive parameters are closely linked to the positional encoding module, particularly in models using Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), where perturbations disrupt dominant frequency activations critical for contextual processing. Furthermore, we show that perturbing ToM-sensitive parameters affects LLMs’ attention mechanism by modulating the angle between queries and keys under positional encoding. These insights provide a deeper understanding of how LLMs acquire social reasoning abilities, bridging AI interpretability with cognitive science.

papers.title: Sensitivity Meets Sparsity: The Impact of Extremely Sparse Parameter Patterns on Theory-of-Mind of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Which parameters in LLMs are sensitive to Theory-of-Mind capabilities, and how do these parameters influence ToM reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to identify extremely sparse ToM-sensitive parameters in LLMs and shows that perturbing them degrades ToM performance, contextual localization, and language understanding by disrupting dominant-frequency activations in RoPE-based positional encoding.
