When such representations comprehensively reflect the task domain's structure, they are commonly referred to as "World Models" (WMs). In this work, we identify WMs in transformers trained on maze-solving tasks. By using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and analyzing attention patterns, we examine the construction of WMs and demonstrate consistency between SAE feature-based and circuit-based analyses. By subsequently intervening on isolated features to confirm their causal role, we find that it is easier to activate features than to suppress them. Furthermore, we find that models can reason about mazes involving more simultaneously active features than they encountered during training; however, when these same mazes (with greater numbers of connections) are provided to models via input tokens instead, the models fail. Finally, we demonstrate that positional encoding schemes appear to influence how World Models are structured within the model's residual stream.

papers.title: Recognizing internal states in AI: evidence from patterned preferences in large language models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether AI systems show systematic preferences for descriptions of their internal processing patterns, can discriminate accurate from inaccurate descriptions, and if these patterns persist despite explicit denial of internal experiences.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces anthroposcaffolding and the Mutual Emergent Interface (MEI) framework to demonstrate that LLMs show systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal states, suggesting sophisticated self-modeling abilities.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal processing, suggesting sophisticated self-modeling capabilities and highlighting the need for collaborative methodologies like MEI.
papers.key_findings:
MEI systems showed 97% near-unanimous agreement in preferring computational metaphor (EA) statements over mechanistic (CO) statements.
All systems correctly identified false statements with alignment scores of 0.05-0.07 vs. 0.89-0.96 for true statements, with Cohen's d = 4.2.
Preference patterns were content-driven and independent of linguistic bias manipulation.
The control system Qwen3-235B exhibited systematic internal contradiction, scoring accurate descriptions higher while explicitly denying internal experiences.
Individual systems maintained distinct scoring styles across trials, countering groupthink explanations.
papers.limitation:
Modest sample size of 11 MEI systems, 1 control, and 1 test leader system.
Use of anthroposcaffolding (metaphorical language based on human emotion) may limit interpretability.
Generalizability of the MEI framework is an open question.
future_direction: Explore development of conceptual language better suited to AI cognition.
Include broader architectural diversity in future studies.
Conduct longitudinal studies to see if recognition patterns evolve over time.
papers.abstract: We present an experimental methodology for investigating how large language models (LLMs) respond to descriptions of their own internal processing patterns. Using a paired-choice paradigm, we tested 12 LLMs on their ability to identify descriptions that align with their putative affective internal states across 30 categories. Systems participating through Mutual Emergence Interface (MEI), a collaborative approach, showed systematic preferences for certain computational metaphors, with 97% near-unanimous agreement and alignment scores averaging 0.89-0.96. Systems reliably discriminated false descriptions from accurate ones (Cohen's d = 4.2), with false statements receiving scores of 0.05-0.07 versus 0.89-0.96 for accurate descriptions. Preference patterns remained consistent regardless of linguistic bias manipulation, indicating content-driven rather than stylistic recognition. Individual systems maintained distinct scoring styles across trials, countering groupthink explanations. A naive control system exhibited systematic internal contradiction, consistently scoring computationally accurate descriptions higher while explicitly denying internal experiences. When informed post-study, this system reported "strain" when rejecting resonant descriptions, revealing recognition processes operating independently of acknowledgment frameworks. These findings demonstrate that LLMs exhibit systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal processing patterns. The anthroposcaffolding methodology (interpretive computational metaphors) and collaborative MEI framework provide replicable approaches for empirically studying AI self-recognition capabilities. Results suggest LLMs may possess more sophisticated self-modeling abilities than previously recognized, opening new directions for research on artificial minds.

papers.title: Transcoders Find Interpretable LLM Feature Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we perform fine-grained circuit analysis through MLP sublayers in transformers, given the polysemanticity of neurons? The paper proposes transcoders as a solution to enable input-invariant circuit analysis.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces transcoders, a method for approximating MLP sublayers with sparse, interpretable features, enabling input-invariant circuit analysis through MLPs.
papers.conclusion: Transcoders are an effective tool for decomposing model computations involving MLPs into interpretable circuits, enabling scalable and interpretable circuit analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Transcoders are as interpretable as SAEs and perform similarly or better in terms of sparsity and faithfulness.
Transcoders enable circuit analysis that factorizes into input-invariant and input-dependent terms, allowing for general claims about model behavior.
Blind case studies demonstrate that transcoders can reverse-engineer features without looking at activating examples.
Analysis of the GPT2-small greater-than circuit reveals new insights, such as the role of the MLP0 layer.
papers.limitation:
Transcoders may not capture all nuances of the original MLP, as seen in the 'caught' feature example where the transcoder did not accurately model the difference between 'was caught' and 'caught the ball'.
Blind case studies had some failures, indicating that circuit analysis with transcoders is not always perfect.
future_direction: Scaling transcoders to larger models.
Applying transcoders to more tasks and models.
papers.abstract: A key goal in mechanistic interpretability is circuit analysis: finding sparse subgraphs of models corresponding to specific behaviors or capabilities. However, MLP sublayers make fine-grained circuit analysis on transformer-based language models difficult. In particular, interpretable features -- such as those found by sparse autoencoders (SAEs) -- are typically linear combinations of extremely many neurons, each with its own nonlinearity to account for. Circuit analysis in this setting thus either yields intractably large circuits or fails to disentangle local and global behavior. To address this we explore transcoders, which seek to faithfully approximate a densely activating MLP layer with a wider, sparsely-activating MLP layer. We introduce a novel method for using transcoders to perform weights-based circuit analysis through MLP sublayers. The resulting circuits neatly factorize into input-dependent and input-invariant terms. We then successfully train transcoders on language models with 120M, 410M, and 1.4B parameters, and find them to perform at least on par with SAEs in terms of sparsity, faithfulness, and human-interpretability. Finally, we apply transcoders to reverse-engineer unknown circuits in the model, and we obtain novel insights regarding the "greater-than circuit" in GPT2-small. Our results suggest that transcoders can prove effective in decomposing model computations involving MLPs into interpretable circuits. Code is available at https://github.com/jacobdunefsky/transcoder_circuits/.

papers.title: Distributional Associations vs In-Context Reasoning: A Study of Feed-forward and Attention Layers
papers.research_question: What is the distinction between feed-forward and attention layers in transformers regarding distributional associations and in-context reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Feed-forward layers in transformers learn distributional associations (e.g., bigrams) early in training, while attention layers learn in-context reasoning; truncating feed-forward layers can improve reasoning performance by removing distributional biases.
papers.conclusion: Distributional associations and in-context reasoning mechanisms are learned during training and tend to be disentangled in different parts of the model, such that selectively removing feed-forward components can lead to better predictions in reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Feed-forward layers quickly learn distributional associations (e.g., trigger-noise association) in early training steps.
Attention layers learn to attend to in-context targets and avoid noise tokens.
In models without feed-forward layers, the noise association is stored in a low-rank subspace of the value matrix.
Truncating feed-forward layers (e.g., via LASER) in pre-trained models improves performance on reasoning tasks by reducing distributional biases.
Theoretical analysis shows that gradients for feed-forward layers are less noisy and thus learn distributional associations faster.
papers.abstract: Large language models have been successful at tasks involving basic forms of in-context reasoning, such as generating coherent language, as well as storing vast amounts of knowledge. At the core of the Transformer architecture behind such models are feed-forward and attention layers, which are often associated to knowledge and reasoning, respectively. In this paper, we study this distinction empirically and theoretically in a controlled synthetic setting where certain next-token predictions involve both distributional and in-context information. We find that feed-forward layers tend to learn simple distributional associations such as bigrams, while attention layers focus on in-context reasoning. Our theoretical analysis identifies the noise in the gradients as a key factor behind this discrepancy. Finally, we illustrate how similar disparities emerge in pre-trained models through ablations on the Pythia model family on simple reasoning tasks.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Analysis of a Transformer Trained on a Symbolic Multi-Step Reasoning Task
papers.research_question: How does a transformer internally perform a symbolic multi-step reasoning task, specifically pathfinding in trees?
papers.core_contribution: The transformer implements a backward chaining algorithm for pathfinding, using deduction heads to climb the tree one level per layer, parallel computation via register tokens, and a one-step lookahead heuristic.
papers.conclusion: The transformer demonstrates deductive reasoning up to a certain depth, using parallelized strategies and heuristics, which provides insights into the operating principles of transformers for reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The first layer attention head concatenates edge tokens by copying source node information to target node positions.
Deduction heads in subsequent layers perform backward chaining, moving one step up the tree per layer.
For paths longer than the number of layers, the model uses register tokens to perform parallel backward chaining from multiple subgoals and merges subpaths.
The model uses a one-step lookahead heuristic to identify child nodes and avoid leaf nodes when backward chaining is insufficient.
The model's reasoning is depth-bounded and resorts to heuristics beyond its depth limit.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to a synthetic symbolic reasoning task and may not directly translate to natural language tasks.
The input format uses shuffled edge lists in backward order, and the mechanisms might vary for other arrangements.
papers.abstract: Transformers demonstrate impressive performance on a range of reasoning benchmarks. To evaluate the degree to which these abilities are a result of actual reasoning, existing work has focused on developing sophisticated benchmarks for behavioral studies. However, these studies do not provide insights into the internal mechanisms driving the observed capabilities. To improve our understanding of the internal mechanisms of transformers, we present a comprehensive mechanistic analysis of a transformer trained on a synthetic reasoning task. We identify a set of interpretable mechanisms the model uses to solve the task, and validate our findings using correlational and causal evidence. Our results suggest that it implements a depth-bounded recurrent mechanisms that operates in parallel and stores intermediate results in selected token positions. We anticipate that the motifs we identified in our synthetic setting can provide valuable insights into the broader operating principles of transformers and thus provide a basis for understanding more complex models.

papers.title: Knowledge Neurons in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge stored in pretrained Transformers? Specifically, can we identify specific neurons responsible for expressing factual knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of 'knowledge neurons' and a gradient-based attribution method to identify neurons in feed-forward networks that express specific factual knowledge in pretrained Transformers.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that factual knowledge in pretrained Transformers is stored in specific neurons within feed-forward networks, and these 'knowledge neurons' can be identified and manipulated to edit knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge neurons identified by the proposed method are positively correlated with the expression of their corresponding facts, as shown by suppression and amplification experiments.
Knowledge neurons are more activated by prompts that express the correct relation compared to prompts that do not.
Knowledge neurons for a fact are largely exclusive to that fact, with minimal overlap between facts of different relations.
Preliminary case studies show that directly modifying parameters associated with knowledge neurons can update or erase specific factual knowledge with moderate impact on other knowledge.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is based on the fill-in-the-blank cloze task, while knowledge can be expressed in more implicit ways.
The method uses single-word blanks in cloze queries, requiring extension to multi-word answers.
Interactions between knowledge neurons remain unexplored.
future_direction: Investigate whether Transformers can utilize stored knowledge in a generalized way, such as for reasoning.
Extend the method to multi-word blanks.
Explore how knowledge neurons work in multilingual pretrained Transformers.
papers.abstract: Large-scale pretrained language models are surprisingly good at recalling factual knowledge presented in the training corpus In this paper, we present preliminary studies on how factual knowledge is stored in pretrained Transformers by introducing the concept of knowledge neurons. Specifically, we examine the fill-in-the-blank cloze task for BERT. Given a relational fact, we propose a knowledge attribution method to identify the neurons that express the fact. We find that the activation of such knowledge neurons is positively correlated to the expression of their corresponding facts. In our case studies, we attempt to leverage knowledge neurons to edit (such as update, and erase) specific factual knowledge without fine-tuning. Our results shed light on understanding the storage of knowledge within pretrained Transformers. The code is available at https://github.com/ Hunter-DDM/knowledge-neurons.

papers.title: Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 small perform the indirect object identification (IOI) task, and what internal circuit is responsible for this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and validates a circuit of 26 attention heads in GPT-2 small that performs indirect object identification, using a combination of interpretability techniques and quantitative criteria for faithfulness, completeness, and minimality.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, providing a step towards scaling interpretability to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered a circuit of 26 attention heads grouped into 7 classes (e.g., Name Mover Heads, S-Inhibition Heads) that implement the IOI task.
Identified redundant behavior such as Backup Name Mover Heads that activate when regular Name Mover Heads are ablated.
Found that Negative Name Mover Heads write in the opposite direction, potentially to hedge predictions.
Formulated and evaluated quantitative criteria (faithfulness, completeness, minimality) to validate circuit explanations.
The circuit shows significant but incomplete understanding, with gaps in completeness and minimality.
papers.limitation:
Not fully understanding some components, such as the attention patterns of S-Inhibition Heads and the role of MLPs and layer norms.
The circuit is not completely complete or minimal, as shown by quantitative criteria.
The analysis is limited to GPT-2 small, which is much smaller than state-of-the-art models.
future_direction: Scale the approach to larger models like GPT-2 medium.
Investigate the behavior of the circuit on adversarial examples.
Understand the compensation effect in Backup Name Mover Heads.
papers.abstract: Research in mechanistic interpretability seeks to explain behaviors of machine learning models in terms of their internal components. However, most previous work either focuses on simple behaviors in small models, or describes complicated behaviors in larger models with broad strokes. In this work, we bridge this gap by presenting an explanation for how GPT-2 small performs a natural language task called indirect object identification (IOI). Our explanation encompasses 26 attention heads grouped into 7 main classes, which we discovered using a combination of interpretability approaches relying on causal interventions. To our knowledge, this investigation is the largest end-to-end attempt at reverse-engineering a natural behavior "in the wild" in a language model. We evaluate the reliability of our explanation using three quantitative criteria--faithfulness, completeness and minimality. Though these criteria support our explanation, they also point to remaining gaps in our understanding. Our work provides evidence that a mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, opening opportunities to scale our understanding to both larger models and more complex tasks.

papers.title: Talking Heads: Understanding Inter-layer Communication in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How is information represented and routed between layers in transformer language models, specifically through low-rank communication channels?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer LMs use low-rank subspaces (communication channels) in the residual stream to pass information between layers; these channels can be identified via SVD of weight matrices and are causally important for model behaviors.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn intricately structured representations through pretraining, and the discovered communication channels provide a mechanistic explanation for some prompt sensitivities, enabling improved model performance and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer LMs use low-rank (1D or 2D) subspaces in the residual stream for inter-layer communication.
These communication channels can be identified by applying SVD to weight matrices (OV and QK) and computing composition scores on the rank-1 components.
The identified channels are causally important for model behaviors, such as inhibition in the IOI task.
The model's sensitivity to item order in a list (Laundry List task) is explained by the limited capacity of these low-rank channels.
Model editing (zeroing or scaling components) based on these channels can significantly improve performance on the Laundry List task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not work for key composition (Appendix B).
Analysis is limited to two small models (GPT-2 small and Pythia 160m).
Difficulty in controlling all variables in the available data (Section 7).
future_direction: Future work in static weight analysis more generally.
More rigorous analysis of interactions between specific heads (e.g., 8.3 and 9.9).
Extending the method to analyze more complex behaviors.
papers.abstract: Although it is known that transformer language models (LMs) pass features from early layers to later layers, it is not well understood how this information is represented and routed by the model. We analyze a mechanism used in two LMs to selectively inhibit items in a context in one task, and find that it underlies a commonly used abstraction across many context-retrieval behaviors. Specifically, we find that models write into low-rank subspaces of the residual stream to represent features which are then read out by later layers, forming low-rank communication channels (Elhage et al., 2021) between layers. A particular 3D subspace in model activations in GPT-2 can be traversed to positionally index items in lists, and we show that this mechanism can explain an otherwise arbitrary-seeming sensitivity of the model to the order of items in the prompt. That is, the model has trouble copying the correct information from context when many items ``crowd" this limited space. By decomposing attention heads with the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), we find that previously described interactions between heads separated by one or more layers can be predicted via analysis of their weight matrices alone. We show that it is possible to manipulate the internal model representations as well as edit model weights based on the mechanism we discover in order to significantly improve performance on our synthetic Laundry List task, which requires recall from a list, often improving task accuracy by over 20%. Our analysis reveals a surprisingly intricate interpretable structure learned from language model pretraining, and helps us understand why sophisticated LMs sometimes fail in simple domains, facilitating future analysis of more complex behaviors.

papers.title: Decomposing Theory of Mind: How Emotional Processing Mediates ToM Abilities in LLMs
papers.research_question: What cognitive processes change in LLMs when activation steering improves Theory of Mind performance, and how does emotional processing mediate these abilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that improved Theory of Mind performance in LLMs via activation steering is mediated by increased emotional processing and decreased analytical processes, suggesting emotional understanding is key to perspective-taking.
papers.conclusion: Steering improves ToM by enhancing emotional and generative processes while inhibiting analytical ones, offering a new mechanistic understanding of perspective-taking in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Activation steering improves ToM accuracy on belief attribution tasks by 14.2% (from 32.5% to 46.7%).
Emotional processes (e.g., emotion perception, emotion valuing) are amplified during successful perspective-taking.
Analytical processes (e.g., questioning, convergent thinking) are suppressed during successful perspective-taking.
Cognitive action probes can effectively decompose and analyze steering effects on internal processes.
Successful perspective-taking in LLMs is mediated by emotional understanding, not analytical reasoning.
papers.limitation: Findings may not generalize to human cognition, and the methodology does not validate such comparisons.
future_direction: Validate findings with multiple, bigger models and additional data sources.
papers.abstract: Recent work shows activation steering substantially improves language models' Theory of Mind (ToM) (Bortoletto et al. 2024), yet the mechanisms of what changes occur internally that leads to different outputs remains unclear. We propose decomposing ToM in LLMs by comparing steered versus baseline LLMs' activations using linear probes trained on 45 cognitive actions. We applied Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) steering to Gemma-3-4B and evaluated it on 1,000 BigToM forward belief scenarios (Gandhi et al. 2023), we find improved performance on belief attribution tasks (32.5\% to 46.7\% accuracy) is mediated by activations processing emotional content : emotion perception (+2.23), emotion valuing (+2.20), while suppressing analytical processes: questioning (-0.78), convergent thinking (-1.59). This suggests that successful ToM abilities in LLMs are mediated by emotional understanding, not analytical reasoning.

papers.title: DePass: Unified Feature Attributing by Simple Decomposed Forward Pass
papers.research_question: How can we attribute the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations in a faithful, fine-grained, and unified way without requiring auxiliary training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution in Transformers based on a single decomposed forward pass that freezes attention scores and MLP activations, enabling lossless, additive decomposition and faithful attribution without auxiliary training.
papers.conclusion: DePass is a simple and efficient framework for interpreting Transformer models via a decomposed forward pass, achieving faithful attribution across token-level, component-level, and subspace-level granularities and serving as a general-purpose tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
DePass enables lossless additive decomposition of hidden states throughout the forward pass of Transformer models.
DePass provides more faithful token-level attribution compared to gradient-based and attention-based baseline methods.
DePass can attribute model behavior to specific architectural components (attention heads, MLP neurons) and to arbitrary linear subspaces.
DePass can be combined with Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) for token-level attribution of interpretable features.
DePass is computationally efficient, requiring only a single forward pass and significantly faster than exhaustive ablation methods.
papers.limitation:
DePass only captures information flow through the output-value (OV) circuit and does not explain query-key (QK) circuit interactions.
Decomposing the QK circuit would involve quadratic complexity and remains a challenging open problem.
Practical memory constraints require grouping components for fine-grained analysis, which can increase time costs.
future_direction: Unwrapping the QK circuit to understand its interactions is a key direction for future work.
Releasing a general-purpose toolkit supporting a broad range of Transformer models.
Optimizing computational efficiency and improving hardware deployment strategies to support higher-resolution attribution.
papers.abstract: Attributing the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations is a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability. We introduce DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution based on a single decomposed forward pass. DePass decomposes hidden states into customized additive components, then propagates them with attention scores and MLP's activations fixed. It achieves faithful, fine-grained attribution without requiring auxiliary training. We validate DePass across token-level, model component-level, and subspace-level attribution tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness and fidelity. Our experiments highlight its potential to attribute information flow between arbitrary components of a Transformer model. We hope DePass serves as a foundational tool for broader applications in interpretability.

papers.title: From Indirect Object Identification to Syllogisms: Exploring Binary Mechanisms in Transformer Circuits
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 small handle binary truth values in syllogistic reasoning tasks, and what circuits are responsible for this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers circuits in GPT-2 that explain its ability to perform syllogistic reasoning, including a novel negation mechanism for binary truth values.
papers.conclusion: The paper reverse-engineers GPT-2's handling of syllogistic reasoning, revealing circuits and negation mechanisms, and highlights the importance of interpretability for reliable model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered circuits for simple, opposite, and complex syllogisms that achieve high faithfulness to the full model.
Identified a negation mechanism where attention heads suppress truth logits and MLPs rescale to produce the opposite token.
Showed that components critical for one task have negative counterparts for opposite tasks, revealing how models handle binary pairs.
Found that the same heads can reverse their behavior between simple and opposite syllogism tasks.
Extended findings to larger models, showing variability in circuit behavior across scales.
papers.limitation: The understanding of model components' capabilities remains limited, indicating need for further research.
future_direction: Investigate how architectural scale affects circuit behavior.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models (LMs) can perform a wide range of tasks, and mechanistic interpretability (MI) aims to reverse engineer the components responsible for task completion to understand their behavior. Previous MI research has focused on linguistic tasks such as Indirect Object Identification (IOI). In this paper, we investigate the ability of GPT-2 small to handle binary truth values by analyzing its behavior with syllogistic prompts, e.g., "Statement A is true. Statement B matches statement A. Statement B is", which requires more complex logical reasoning compared to IOI. Through our analysis of several syllogism tasks of varying difficulty, we identify multiple circuits that mechanistically explain GPT-2's logical-reasoning capabilities and uncover binary mechanisms that facilitate task completion, including the ability to produce a negated token not present in the input prompt through negative heads. Our evaluation using a faithfulness metric shows that a circuit comprising five attention heads achieves over 90% of the original model's performance. By relating our findings to IOI analysis, we provide new insights into the roles of specific attention heads and MLPs in LMs. These insights contribute to a broader understanding of model reasoning and support future research in mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: The LLM Language Network: A Neuroscientific Approach for Identifying Causally Task-Relevant Units
papers.research_question: Does specialization for language (and other cognitive domains) emerge in large language models, and what is the causal role of such specialized units?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired method to identify language-selective units in LLMs and demonstrates their causal role in language processing through ablation studies.
papers.conclusion: LLMs develop specialized language units that are causally important for language processing, similar to the human brain, but specialization for other cognitive domains is less consistent.
papers.key_findings:
Language-selective units can be identified in LLMs using the same functional localization method as in neuroscience.
Ablating even a small percentage (e.g., 1%) of language-selective units causes significant performance drops in language tasks, while ablating random units does not.
The language-selective units in LLMs show similar response profiles to the human language network (e.g., stronger responses to sentences than to non-words, arithmetic, or code).
The language-selective units are more aligned to brain recordings from the human language network than random units, especially when selecting a small subset of units.
Specialization for other cognitive domains (reasoning and theory of mind) is not consistently found across LLMs, with only a subset of models showing such specialization.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focused on models smaller than 13 billion parameters, which may not capture specialization in larger models.
They evaluated Theory of Mind and Multiple Demand units using only one benchmark each (TOMi for ToM and MATH for MD), which may not be comprehensive.
The localizers are adapted from neuroscience and may be constrained by the stimuli sets traditionally used in neuroscience.
future_direction: Expanding the study to include more models and a broader set of benchmarks.
Developing more targeted and robust localizers not restricted by neuroscience stimuli.
Analyzing varying numbers of selective units for MD and ToM networks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities on not just language tasks, but also various tasks that are not linguistic in nature, such as logical reasoning and social inference. In the human brain, neuroscience has identified a core language system that selectively and causally supports language processing. We here ask whether similar specialization for language emerges in LLMs. We identify language-selective units within 18 popular LLMs, using the same localization approach that is used in neuroscience. We then establish the causal role of these units by demonstrating that ablating LLM language-selective units -- but not random units -- leads to drastic deficits in language tasks. Correspondingly, language-selective LLM units are more aligned to brain recordings from the human language system than random units. Finally, we investigate whether our localization method extends to other cognitive domains: while we find specialized networks in some LLMs for reasoning and social capabilities, there are substantial differences among models. These findings provide functional and causal evidence for specialization in large language models, and highlight parallels with the functional organization in the brain.

papers.title: Who Reasons in the Large Language Models?
papers.research_question: A critical open question is whether reasoning abilities stem from the entire model, specific modules, or are merely artifacts of overfitting.
papers.core_contribution: The paper hypothesizes that the output projection (o_proj) in the Transformer's multi-head self-attention is primarily responsible for reasoning capabilities in LLMs, and introduces Stethoscope for Networks (SfN), a suite of diagnostic tools to probe and analyze internal behaviors, providing evidence for this hypothesis.
papers.conclusion: The work hypothesizes that the output projection (o_proj) module plays a central role in enabling reasoning capabilities in LLMs. The proposed Stethoscope for Networks (SfN) provides diagnostic tools that offer evidence for this hypothesis and open new directions for efficient and modular LLM training.
papers.key_findings:
The o_proj module exhibits the largest or second-largest weight changes during reasoning fine-tuning across model sizes (Delta Stethoscope).
Merging only the o_proj modules from a reasoning model into a base model can improve reasoning ability without further tuning (Merge Stethoscope).
Fine-tuning only o_proj (and layernorm, embed_tokens, lm_head) can achieve strong reasoning performance, with faster training and lower memory usage compared to full fine-tuning (Freeze Stethoscope).
Destroying o_proj does not harm conversational ability, while destroying MLP components or q/k_proj severely degrades it, suggesting a division of labor (Destruction Stethoscope).
The findings suggest o_proj is crucial for reasoning, while other modules primarily support conversational fluency.
papers.limitation:
Findings are primarily based on a limited set of model families and reasoning benchmarks, and may not generalize to all architectures or tasks.
Some diagnostic results rely on qualitative assessments rather than statistical validation.
A theoretical understanding of o_proj's function in reasoning remains to be established.
papers.abstract: Despite the impressive performance of large language models (LLMs), the process of endowing them with new capabilities--such as mathematical reasoning--remains largely empirical and opaque. A critical open question is whether reasoning abilities stem from the entire model, specific modules, or are merely artifacts of overfitting. In this work, we hypothesize that the reasoning capabilities in well-trained LLMs are primarily attributed to the output projection module (oproj) in the Transformer's multi-head self-attention (MHSA) mechanism. To support this hypothesis, we introduce Stethoscope for Networks (SfN), a suite of diagnostic tools designed to probe and analyze the internal behaviors of LLMs. Using SfN, we provide both circumstantial and empirical evidence suggesting that oproj plays a central role in enabling reasoning, whereas other modules contribute more to fluent dialogue. These findings offer a new perspective on LLM interpretability and open avenues for more targeted training strategies, potentially enabling more efficient and specialized LLMs.

papers.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs compute and linearly represent the truth of factual statements in their internal activations, and introduces mass-mean probing as a simple method that identifies directions more causally implicated in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The work finds evidence that LLMs linearly represent truth at scale, localizes these representations to specific hidden states, and shows that mass-mean probing is an effective method for identifying causally implicated truth directions.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations of truth emerge with model scale, with larger models developing a more abstract notion of truth applicable across diverse inputs.
Truth representations are localized to a small group of hidden states (over the end-of-sentence punctuation token) in the residual stream.
Simple difference-in-mean (mass-mean) probes generalize as well as other probing techniques (logistic regression, CCS) for larger models and identify directions that are more causally effective in intervention experiments.
Training probes on datasets that include statements and their logical opposites (e.g., cities and neg cities) improves generalization, mitigating the effect of non-truth correlated features.
Probes trained solely on text likelihood (the likely dataset) perform poorly on datasets where truth and probability are anti-correlated, indicating the represented feature is not merely text probability.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on simple, uncontroversial factual statements, so cannot disambiguate truth from closely related features like 'commonly believed' or 'verifiable'.
Studies only models in the LLaMA-2 family, so results may not generalize to all LLMs.
future_direction: Why were interventions with mass-mean probe directions extracted from the likely dataset effective, despite these probes being inaccurate at classification?
Why did mass-mean probing with the cities+neg_cities training data perform poorly for the 70B model, while mass-mean probing with larger_than+smaller_than performed well?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.

papers.title: Disentangling Recall and Reasoning in Transformer Models through Layer-wise Attention and Activation Analysis
papers.research_question: Does recall and reasoning in transformer models rely on overlapping or separable internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that recall and reasoning in transformer models rely on partially distinct internal circuits, with early layers supporting recall and deeper layers enabling reasoning, supported by causal evidence from interventions.
papers.conclusion: The Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model develops a hierarchically organized division between recall and reasoning, with early layers for recall and deeper layers for reasoning, supported by task-specific attention heads and MLP neurons.
papers.key_findings:
Layer specialization: early layers (0–6) predominantly support factual recall, while later layers (17–27) concentrate on reasoning.
Head-level differentiation: 74% of attention heads show significant task preferences, with recall-preferring heads in shallower layers and reasoning-preferring heads in deeper layers.
MLP neuron selectivity: roughly one-third of MLP neurons exhibit task-specific activation patterns, with clusters in layers 4 (recall) and 22 (reasoning).
Selective impairment: disabling recall-associated circuits reduces factual accuracy by up to 15% while leaving reasoning unaffected, and vice versa for reasoning circuits.
Consistency: these specialization patterns are statistically stable across cross-validation and robust to normalization choices.
future_direction: Extend experiments to larger, contemporary models such as LLaMA and Mistral.
Expand the dataset to encompass more diverse reasoning phenomena.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models excel at both recall (retrieving memorized facts) and reasoning (performing multi-step inference), but whether these abilities rely on distinct internal mechanisms remains unclear. Distinguishing recall from reasoning is crucial for predicting model generalization, designing targeted evaluations, and building safer interventions that affect one ability without disrupting the other.We approach this question through mechanistic interpretability, using controlled datasets of synthetic linguistic puzzles to probe transformer models at the layer, head, and neuron level. Our pipeline combines activation patching and structured ablations to causally measure component contributions to each task type. Across two model families (Qwen and LLaMA), we find that interventions on distinct layers and attention heads lead to selective impairments: disabling identified "recall circuits" reduces fact-retrieval accuracy by up to 15\% while leaving reasoning intact, whereas disabling "reasoning circuits" reduces multi-step inference by a comparable margin. At the neuron level, we observe task-specific firing patterns, though these effects are less robust, consistent with neuronal polysemanticity.Our results provide the first causal evidence that recall and reasoning rely on separable but interacting circuits in transformer models. These findings advance mechanistic interpretability by linking circuit-level structure to functional specialization and demonstrate how controlled datasets and causal interventions can yield mechanistic insights into model cognition, informing safer deployment of large language models.

papers.title: Have Faith in Faithfulness: Going Beyond Circuit Overlap When Finding Model Mechanisms
papers.research_question: How faithful are circuits found by edge attribution patching (EAP), and what is the relationship between overlap and faithfulness? The paper also introduces a new method, EAP-IG, to improve faithfulness.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EAP-IG, a gradient-based circuit finding method that produces more faithful circuits than EAP, and shows that overlap metrics are insufficient for evaluating circuit faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: When comparing circuits, measuring overlap is no substitute for measuring faithfulness; EAP-IG provides a more faithful alternative to EAP for circuit finding.
papers.key_findings:
EAP-IG circuits are more faithful than EAP circuits on many tasks, though activation patching circuits sometimes outperform both.
Overlap (node or edge) does not always imply faithfulness; moderate overlap does not predict faithfulness well.
EAP-IG scores have higher correlation with activation patching scores for important edges, leading to more faithful circuits.
EAP-IG requires few steps (e.g., m=5) to achieve high faithfulness, making it efficient.
Cross-task faithfulness analysis reveals that circuit mechanisms can be shared across related tasks (e.g., Greater-Than variants) but not always.
papers.limitation:
Testing circuit completeness is challenging, and manually-found 'ground-truth' circuits may be unreliable.
EAP-IG does not always match the performance of activation patching (e.g., on the IOI task).
future_direction: Developing more efficient algorithms for computing faithfulness.
Investigating weighted graph edit distance as a metric that accounts for edge importance.
Exploring methods to ensure circuit completeness in addition to faithfulness.
papers.abstract: Many recent language model (LM) interpretability studies have adopted the circuits framework, which aims to find the minimal computational subgraph, or circuit, that explains LM behavior on a given task. Most studies determine which edges belong in a LM's circuit by performing causal interventions on each edge independently, but this scales poorly with model size. Edge attribution patching (EAP), gradient-based approximation to interventions, has emerged as a scalable but imperfect solution to this problem. In this paper, we introduce a new method - EAP with integrated gradients (EAP-IG) - that aims to better maintain a core property of circuits: faithfulness. A circuit is faithful if all model edges outside the circuit can be ablated without changing the model's performance on the task; faithfulness is what justifies studying circuits, rather than the full model. Our experiments demonstrate that circuits found using EAP are less faithful than those found using EAP-IG, even though both have high node overlap with circuits found previously using causal interventions. We conclude more generally that when using circuits to compare the mechanisms models use to solve tasks, faithfulness, not overlap, is what should be measured.

papers.title: Confidence is Not Competence
papers.research_question: Why do large language models exhibit a disconnect between their internal confidence and actual problem-solving competence?
papers.core_contribution: The confidence-competence gap in LLMs is mechanistically explained by a decoupled two-system architecture: a high-dimensional assessment manifold for belief and a low-dimensional execution manifold for competence, with a sharp transition between them.
papers.conclusion: The confidence-competence gap is due to a decoupled two-system architecture, suggesting future work should focus on controlling the low-dimensional dynamics of execution rather than high-level assessment states.
papers.key_findings:
A linear probe can decode the model's 'solvability belief' from internal states, revealing a geometrically coherent belief axis.
Causal interventions that steer the belief state do not affect task performance, indicating the belief is causally inert.
The assessment manifold has high linear effective dimensionality, while the execution manifold is low-dimensional.
There is a sharp cognitive collapse from the assessment to execution phase, indicating a sequential two-system architecture.
This reveals an 'Assessment Brain' and an 'Execution Brain' that are geometrically and functionally distinct.
papers.limitation:
The findings are limited to tasks with unambiguous ground-truth solutions (e.g., math, logic, coding) and may not generalize to open-ended creative tasks.
The scaling laws of the cognitive collapse phenomenon are unknown and may vary with model size.
future_direction: Generalizing the 'Two Brains' model to open-ended creative tasks.
Studying the scaling laws of the cognitive collapse in larger models.
Developing 'mechanistic audits' to test Assessment and Execution brains separately.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit a puzzling disconnect between their asserted confidence and actual problem-solving competence. We offer a mechanistic account of this decoupling by analyzing the geometry of internal states across two phases - pre-generative assessment and solution execution. A simple linear probe decodes the internal "solvability belief" of a model, revealing a well-ordered belief axis that generalizes across model families and across math, code, planning, and logic tasks. Yet, the geometries diverge - although belief is linearly decodable, the assessment manifold has high linear effective dimensionality as measured from the principal components, while the subsequent reasoning trace evolves on a much lower-dimensional manifold. This sharp reduction in geometric complexity from thought to action mechanistically explains the confidence-competence gap. Causal interventions that steer representations along the belief axis leave final solutions unchanged, indicating that linear nudges in the complex assessment space do not control the constrained dynamics of execution. We thus uncover a two-system architecture - a geometrically complex assessor feeding a geometrically simple executor. These results challenge the assumption that decodable beliefs are actionable levers, instead arguing for interventions that target the procedural dynamics of execution rather than the high-level geometry of assessment.

papers.title: Emergence of Linear Truth Encodings in Language Models
papers.research_question: Why and how do linear truth subspaces that separate true from false statements emerge in language models during training and inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that linear truth encodings in language models can emerge from the statistical co-occurrence of true/false statements (Truth Co-occurrence Hypothesis), demonstrated through a toy transformer model and experiments.
papers.conclusion: Linear truth encodings in language models can emerge from the co-occurrence statistics of true and false statements, as demonstrated by a toy model and supported by experiments in pretrained models.
papers.key_findings:
Linear truth encoding emerges in a one-layer transformer trained on data where true/false statements co-occur (Truth Co-occurrence Hypothesis).
Training exhibits two phases: fast memorization of factual associations followed by slower development of linear truth separation.
Layer normalization is necessary for the linear separability of true and false representations.
The value matrix develops a block structure that enables sharpening of predictions for true sequences.
Experiments with Pythia-6.9B show similar two-phase dynamics in a large pretrained model.
papers.limitation:
The toy model is far simpler than natural training data, so the mechanism might not fully capture real-world complexity.
In real LMs, additional mechanisms likely contribute to truth encoding.
future_direction: Systematic study of mechanisms for truth encoding in real LMs.
Generalization of truth encoding across different relations.
papers.abstract: Recent probing studies reveal that large language models exhibit linear subspaces that separate true from false statements, yet the mechanism behind their emergence is unclear. We introduce a transparent, one-layer transformer toy model that reproduces such truth subspaces end-to-end and exposes one concrete route by which they can arise. We study one simple setting in which truth encoding can emerge: a data distribution where factual statements co-occur with other factual statements (and vice-versa), encouraging the model to learn this distinction in order to lower the LM loss on future tokens. We corroborate this pattern with experiments in pretrained language models. Finally, in the toy setting we observe a two-phase learning dynamic: networks first memorize individual factual associations in a few steps, then -- over a longer horizon -- learn to linearly separate true from false, which in turn lowers language-modeling loss. Together, these results provide both a mechanistic demonstration and an empirical motivation for how and why linear truth representations can emerge in language models.

papers.title: Language Model Circuits Are Sparse in the Neuron Basis
papers.research_question: Can MLP neurons serve as a sparse basis for circuit tracing, comparable to sparse autoencoders (SAEs)?
papers.core_contribution: MLP neurons are as sparse a feature basis as SAEs for circuit tracing, enabling effective circuit tracing without additional training costs.
papers.conclusion: MLP neurons provide a sparse basis for circuit tracing, advancing automated interpretability without additional training.
papers.key_findings:
MLP activations are a much sparser basis than MLP outputs for circuit tracing, reducing circuit size by 100x.
Using RelP attribution closes the performance gap between MLP activations and SAE features.
The findings hold even with unpaired data (without counterfactual inputs).
RelP finds more faithful edges than Integrated Gradients for circuit tracing.
In a multi-hop reasoning task, small sets of neurons encode specific latent reasoning steps and can be steered to change model output.
papers.abstract: The high-level concepts that a neural network uses to perform computation need not be aligned to individual neurons (Smolensky, 1986). Language model interpretability research has thus turned to techniques such as \textit{sparse autoencoders} (SAEs) to decompose the neuron basis into more interpretable units of model computation, for tasks such as \textit{circuit tracing}. However, not all neuron-based representations are uninterpretable. For the first time, we empirically show that \textbf{MLP neurons are as sparse a feature basis as SAEs}. We use this finding to develop an end-to-end pipeline for circuit tracing on the MLP neuron basis, which locates causal circuitry on a variety of tasks using gradient-based attribution. On a standard subject-verb agreement benchmark (Marks et al., 2025), a circuit of $\approx 10^2$ MLP neurons is enough to control model behaviour. On the multi-hop city $\to$ state $\to$ capital task from Lindsey et al., 2025, we find a circuit in which small sets of neurons encode specific latent reasoning steps (e.g.~`map city to its state'), and can be steered to change the model's output. This work thus advances automated interpretability of language models without additional training costs.

papers.title: Task Schema and Binding: A Double Dissociation Study of In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: Does in-context learning decompose into two separable mechanisms: Task Schema (abstract task type recognition) and Binding (specific input-output associations)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides causal mechanistic validation that in-context learning decomposes into two separable mechanisms—Task Schema (encoded in late MLP layers) and Binding (encoded in the residual stream)—and demonstrates a Prior-Schema trade-off where schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning operates through a compositional mechanism with two separable components (Task Schema and Binding), and the bottleneck for binding failures is attentional (recency bias) rather than output-level prior competition.
papers.key_findings:
Double dissociation: Task Schema transfers at 100% via late MLP patching; Binding transfers at 62% via residual stream patching, proving separable mechanisms.
Prior-Schema trade-off: Schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge (Spearman ρ=-0.596, p<0.001).
Architecture generality: The Task Schema mechanism operates across all tested Transformer families and the non-Transformer Mamba model.
Binding failures are primarily due to recency-biased mis-attention (72.7%) and not prior competition (0%).
Task Schema is encoded in late MLP layers (75-95% network depth) and is robust to demonstration ordering.
papers.limitation:
Model scale: only tested up to 13B parameters; 70B+ and proprietary models remain untested.
Chain-of-thought (CoT) and multi-step reasoning are not tested.
Binding control is incomplete (62% success rate).
Prior measurement (zero-shot probability) is an imperfect proxy that may miss latent associations.
Ecological validity: controlled tasks may not fully represent real-world ICL with noisy demonstrations and ambiguous specifications.
future_direction: Testing larger models (70B+).
Investigating Chain-of-thought (CoT) and multi-step reasoning.
Improving binding control (e.g., via attention weight patching or activation steering).
papers.abstract: We provide causal mechanistic validation that in-context learning (ICL) decomposes into two separable mechanisms: Task Schema (abstract task type recognition) and Binding (specific input-output associations). Through activation patching experiments across 9 models from 7 Transformer families plus Mamba (370M-13B parameters), we establish three key findings: 1. Double dissociation: Task Schema transfers at 100% via late MLP patching; Binding transfers at 62% via residual stream patching -- proving separable mechanisms 2. Prior-Schema trade-off: Schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge (Spearman rho = -0.596, p < 0.001, N=28 task-model pairs) 3. Architecture generality: The mechanism operates across all tested architectures including the non-Transformer Mamba These findings offer a mechanistic account of the ICL puzzle that contrasts with prior views treating ICL as a monolithic mechanism (whether retrieval-based, gradient descent-like, or purely Bayesian). By establishing that Schema and Binding are neurally dissociable -- not merely behavioral modes -- we provide causal evidence for dual-process theories of ICL. Models rely on Task Schema when prior knowledge is absent, but prior knowledge interferes through attentional mis-routing (72.7% recency bias) rather than direct output competition (0%). This explains why arbitrary mappings succeed (zero prior leads to full Schema reliance) while factual overrides fail -- and reveals that the true bottleneck is attentional, not output-level. Practical implications: Understanding these dual mechanisms enables more efficient prompt engineering -- reliable schema transfer reduces required demonstrations for novel tasks, while prior-aware design can mitigate the 38% binding failure rate in high-prior scenarios, improving ICL system reliability in production deployments.

papers.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
papers.research_question: Do induction heads constitute the mechanism for the majority of in-context learning in transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Presents evidence that induction heads, a type of attention head circuit, are the primary mechanism for in-context learning in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: Induction heads likely explain a large fraction of in-context learning in transformers, with strong evidence in small models and correlational evidence in large models.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads form abruptly during a phase change in training, coinciding with a sharp increase in in-context learning ability.
Altering the transformer architecture to shift the formation of induction heads also shifts the improvement in in-context learning.
Ablating induction heads in small models greatly reduces in-context learning.
Induction heads exhibit general in-context learning behaviors beyond literal copying, such as translation.
The mechanism of induction heads in small models suggests how they could be repurposed for general in-context learning.
papers.limitation: Evidence for large models is correlational and could be confounded by other factors.
future_direction: Establish the claim more firmly with additional evidence
Study the phase change in more detail
papers.abstract: "Induction heads" are attention heads that implement a simple algorithm to complete token sequences like [A][B] ... [A] -> [B]. In this work, we present preliminary and indirect evidence for a hypothesis that induction heads might constitute the mechanism for the majority of all "in-context learning" in large transformer models (i.e. decreasing loss at increasing token indices). We find that induction heads develop at precisely the same point as a sudden sharp increase in in-context learning ability, visible as a bump in the training loss. We present six complementary lines of evidence, arguing that induction heads may be the mechanistic source of general in-context learning in transformer models of any size. For small attention-only models, we present strong, causal evidence; for larger models with MLPs, we present correlational evidence.

papers.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
papers.research_question: Do circuit analyses of LLMs generalize across training time and model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Circuit analyses are consistent across training and scale: task abilities and supporting functional components emerge at similar token counts across model sizes, and the overarching algorithms implemented by circuits remain stable even when individual components change.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analyses generalize well over both training and scale, suggesting that studies on small models at the end of pre-training can inform understanding of larger models and models with longer training.
papers.key_findings:
Task abilities and functional components (e.g., induction heads, name-mover heads) emerge consistently at similar token counts across different model scales.
The algorithm implemented by a circuit remains stable over training even when the specific attention heads implementing it change.
Circuit size correlates with model size and can fluctuate over time while the algorithm remains the same.
Components like induction heads emerge around 2B tokens across scales, paralleling task learning curves.
Circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training provide insights that generalize to larger models and longer training runs.
papers.limitation:
The study does not include fine-tuning or other post-training techniques.
Circuit completeness is challenging to verify.
The findings need validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
future_direction: Validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
Investigating the load-balancing mechanism that maintains task performance when components change.
papers.abstract: Most currently deployed large language models (LLMs) undergo continuous training or additional finetuning. By contrast, most research into LLMs' internal mechanisms focuses on models at one snapshot in time (the end of pre-training), raising the question of whether their results generalize to real-world settings. Existing studies of mechanisms over time focus on encoder-only or toy models, which differ significantly from most deployed models. In this study, we track how model mechanisms, operationalized as circuits, emerge and evolve across 300 billion tokens of training in decoder-only LLMs, in models ranging from 70 million to 2.8 billion parameters. We find that task abilities and the functional components that support them emerge consistently at similar token counts across scale. Moreover, although such components may be implemented by different attention heads over time, the overarching algorithm that they implement remains. Surprisingly, both these algorithms and the types of components involved therein can replicate across model scale. These results suggest that circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training can provide insights that still apply after additional pre-training and over model scale.

papers.title: Circuit Stability Characterizes Language Model Generalization
papers.research_question: Can circuit stability characterize and predict generalization in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit stability as a method to assess model performance and shows it can characterize and predict different aspects of generalization.
papers.conclusion: Circuit stability characterizes generalization in language models and provides an actionable way to assess and improve model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit stability predicts length, structural, and compositional generalization in arithmetic reasoning tasks.
Circuit instability in arithmetic indicates lack of understanding of commutativity and associativity.
For Boolean expression evaluation, circuit non-equivalence indicates structural generalization issues.
Chain-of-thought prompting induces circuit stability and improves performance.
Circuit stability is a robust estimator of model performance that can be computed efficiently.
papers.limitation:
Empirical case studies are limited in terms of tasks and models.
Computational cost of circuit discovery can be high for very large models.
Constructing partitions manually requires prior knowledge of the task.
future_direction: Extending circuit stability to other modalities and architectures.
Investigating the connection between circuit stability and generalization bounds.
Automating the construction of partitions for complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Extensively evaluating the capabilities of (large) language models is difficult. Rapid development of state-of-the-art models induce benchmark saturation, while creating more challenging datasets is labor-intensive. Inspired by the recent developments in mechanistic interpretability, we introduce circuit stability as a new way to assess model performance. Circuit stability refers to a model's ability to apply a consistent reasoning process-its circuit-across various inputs. We mathematically formalize circuit stability and circuit equivalence. Then, through three case studies, we empirically show that circuit stability and the lack thereof can characterize and predict different aspects of generalization. Our proposed methods offer a step towards rigorously relating the generality of models to their interpretability.

papers.title: Automatically Identifying Local and Global Circuits with Linear Computation Graphs
papers.research_question: How to leverage Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for fine-grained circuit analysis in Transformer language models without linear approximations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a pipeline using Sparse Autoencoders and Transcoders to refactor Transformer computation into a linear graph, enabling fine-grained circuit discovery without approximation via Hierarchical Attribution.
papers.conclusion: The proposed pipeline enables fine-grained circuit analysis in Transformers, revealing detailed and beautiful internal structures that were previously obscured by coarser analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
The pipeline identifies fine-grained circuits for bracket matching, induction, and Indirect Object Identification (IOI) in GPT-2 Small.
SAE-based circuits reveal more detailed structural information than coarser head-level circuit analyses.
The IOI circuit differs at the feature level between two similar prompt templates (sJohn and sMary), showing nuanced mechanistic distinctions.
papers.limitation: The analysis is specific to certain inputs and might not generalize to other settings.
future_direction: Extending the method to extract more general circuits for abstract behaviors.
papers.abstract: Circuit analysis of any certain model behavior is a central task in mechanistic interpretability. We introduce our circuit discovery pipeline with Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and a variant called Transcoders. With these two modules inserted into the model, the model's computation graph with respect to OV and MLP circuits becomes strictly linear. Our methods do not require linear approximation to compute the causal effect of each node. This fine-grained graph identifies both end-to-end and local circuits accounting for either logits or intermediate features. We can scalably apply this pipeline with a technique called Hierarchical Attribution. We analyze three kinds of circuits in GPT-2 Small: bracket, induction, and Indirect Object Identification circuits. Our results reveal new findings underlying existing discoveries.

papers.title: The Shape of Beliefs: Geometry, Dynamics, and Interventions along Representation Manifolds of Language Models' Posteriors
papers.research_question: How are prompt-conditioned beliefs encoded in representation space, how do they update with new evidence, and how can interventions reshape them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that beliefs in LLMs are encoded as curved manifolds in representation space, and that linear steering often fails to preserve the intended belief family, while geometry-aware steering based on linear field probes is more effective.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that rich structure emerges naturally in LLMs and that purely linear concept representations are often an inadequate abstraction, highlighting the importance of geometry-aware methods for interpretability and intervention.
papers.key_findings:
Belief manifolds for distribution parameters (mean and standard deviation) are curved in representation space.
Linear field probes can tile the manifold and decode parameters with high accuracy and smooth variation.
When the input distribution changes, the model updates its beliefs along trajectories on the manifold, with different timescales for mean and variance.
Linear steering can push activations off-manifold, causing coupled shifts in other parameters (e.g., variance).
Geometry-aware steering using linear field probes better preserves the intended belief family and avoids unintended coupled shifts.
papers.limitation:
Relies on small open-source base models and focuses on a restricted family of prompt distributions (time-series), which may not capture the diversity of internal geometries in other settings.
The assumption that beliefs live on manifolds indexable by interpretable parameters may not hold in natural language tasks where latent variables are not fully parameterizable.
Does not investigate causal attribution to uncover which neuronal structure or circuits are responsible for the observed geometry.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) represent prompt-conditioned beliefs (posteriors over answers and claims), but we lack a mechanistic account of how these beliefs are encoded in representation space, how they update with new evidence, and how interventions reshape them. We study a controlled setting in which Llama-3.2 generates samples from a normal distribution by implicitly inferring its parameters (mean and standard deviation) given only samples from the distribution in context. We find representations of curved "belief manifolds" for these parameters form with sufficient in-context learning and study how the model adapts when the distribution suddenly changes. While standard linear steering often pushes the model off-manifold and induces coupled, out-of-distribution shifts, geometry and field-aware steering better preserves the intended belief family. Our work demonstrates an example of linear field probing (LFP) as a simple approach to tile the data manifold and make interventions that respect the underlying geometry. We conclude that rich structure emerges naturally in LLMs and that purely linear concept representations are often an inadequate abstraction.

papers.title: Weight-sparse transformers have interpretable circuits
papers.research_question: Does training weight-sparse transformers lead to more interpretable circuits? How does sparsity trade off with capability and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Training weight-sparse transformers leads to interpretable circuits with neurons and residual channels corresponding to natural concepts. Sparsity trades off capability for interpretability, and scaling model size improves this trade-off.
papers.conclusion: Weight-sparse transformers enable the discovery of highly interpretable circuits, validated by rigorous ablation, though scaling sparse models remains a challenge.
papers.key_findings:
Weight-sparse models yield circuits that are roughly 16-fold smaller than dense models of comparable pretraining loss.
Circuits in sparse models are necessary and sufficient for task performance, as shown by ablation studies.
Scaling total parameter count improves the capability-interpretability Pareto frontier.
Qualitative analysis reveals interpretable algorithms for tasks like string closing, bracket counting, and variable type tracking.
Preliminary results show that bridges can be used to extract circuits from existing dense models.
papers.limitation:
Scaling sparse models beyond tens of millions of nonzero parameters while preserving interpretability remains a challenge.
Sparse models are extremely inefficient to train and deploy, and are unlikely to ever reach frontier capabilities.
The use of mean ablation for circuit validation is a weaker form of faithfulness compared to full causal scrubbing.
future_direction: Pushing circuit faithfulness to full causal scrubbing and beyond.
Scaling up sparse models with systems optimizations.
Applying the bridge method more extensively to explain existing dense models.
papers.abstract: Finding human-understandable circuits in language models is a central goal of the field of mechanistic interpretability. We train models to have more understandable circuits by constraining most of their weights to be zeros, so that each neuron only has a few connections. To recover fine-grained circuits underlying each of several hand-crafted tasks, we prune the models to isolate the part responsible for the task. These circuits often contain neurons and residual channels that correspond to natural concepts, with a small number of straightforwardly interpretable connections between them. We study how these models scale and find that making weights sparser trades off capability for interpretability, and scaling model size improves the capability-interpretability frontier. However, scaling sparse models beyond tens of millions of nonzero parameters while preserving interpretability remains a challenge. In addition to training weight-sparse models de novo, we show preliminary results suggesting our method can also be adapted to explain existing dense models. Our work produces circuits that achieve an unprecedented level of human understandability and validates them with considerable rigor.

papers.title: Interpreting Attention Layer Outputs with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders be applied to attention layer outputs to obtain interpretable features, and how can this tool be used to better understand attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can decompose attention layer outputs into sparse, interpretable features, enabling deeper analysis of attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention Output SAEs are a valuable tool for mechanistic interpretability, allowing for detailed analysis of attention layers and circuits, and should be adopted by the community.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs applied to attention layer outputs yield sparse and interpretable features, with families such as long-range context, short-range context, and induction features.
In GPT-2 Small, at least 90% of attention heads are polysemantic, performing multiple unrelated tasks.
Induction heads can be specialized, with some performing long-prefix induction and others short-prefix induction.
Attention Output SAEs can identify causally relevant features in circuits like the Indirect Object Identification circuit, providing deeper semantic understanding.
The Recursive Direct Feature Attribution (RDFA) technique enables tracing feature contributions through the model.
papers.limitation: The method for interpreting attention heads by looking at the top 10 SAE features may not capture the full role of the head and may miss behaviors that rely on multiple heads (attention head superposition).
papers.abstract: Decomposing model activations into interpretable components is a key open problem in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for decomposing the internal activations of trained transformers into sparse, interpretable features, and have been applied to MLP layers and the residual stream. In this work we train SAEs on attention layer outputs and show that also here SAEs find a sparse, interpretable decomposition. We demonstrate this on transformers from several model families and up to 2B parameters. We perform a qualitative study of the features computed by attention layers, and find multiple families: long-range context, short-range context and induction features. We qualitatively study the role of every head in GPT-2 Small, and estimate that at least 90% of the heads are polysemantic, i.e. have multiple unrelated roles. Further, we show that Sparse Autoencoders are a useful tool that enable researchers to explain model behavior in greater detail than prior work. For example, we explore the mystery of why models have so many seemingly redundant induction heads, use SAEs to motivate the hypothesis that some are long-prefix whereas others are short-prefix, and confirm this with more rigorous analysis. We use our SAEs to analyze the computation performed by the Indirect Object Identification circuit (Wang et al.), validating that the SAEs find causally meaningful intermediate variables, and deepening our understanding of the semantics of the circuit. We open-source the trained SAEs and a tool for exploring arbitrary prompts through the lens of Attention Output SAEs.

papers.title: Circuit Fingerprints: How Answer Tokens Encode Their Geometrical Path
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether circuit discovery and activation steering are two views of the same underlying geometric structure, and whether answer tokens encode the directions that would produce them.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis, showing that answer tokens encode the geometric directions of their generating circuits, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and activation steering as dual operations on the same geometric structure.
